about: Circulation and Breathing (MBBS0015) is the third of the four modules taken in UCL's MBBS Year 1, running across Terms 1 and 2 (in 2026–27, from December to early February, between CIF Weeks A and B). UCL's module page says it introduces the cardiovascular and respiratory systems: how we breathe, how oxygen and nutrients reach the tissues, how waste is removed, and the drugs used to treat disorders of these systems. Its aims also cover responses to changing metabolic demand, the origins and risk factors of common diseases, basic clinical skills and tests, and an introduction to clinical decision-making. The module is taught in person and carries 0 credits; Year 1 knowledge is tested in the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests (online SBA and VSA papers). This pack is educational revision material, not clinical advice, and gives no drug doses.

notes.h: Respiratory structure and the mechanics of breathing
notes.overview: Air moves because the chest changes volume. Quiet inspiration is active muscle work; quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil. This topic links airway anatomy, the pleural coupling of lung to chest wall, compliance and surfactant, and the lung-volume and ventilation calculations used throughout the module.
objectives: Explain why quiet inspiration is active and quiet expiration passive, using Boyle's law and elastic recoil.
Distinguish the conducting and respiratory zones and explain anatomical dead space.
Apply the alveolar ventilation equation to compare breathing patterns.
Explain how compliance and surfactant change in fibrosis, emphysema and prematurity.
Interpret why residual volume and FRC cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

sections.body:
Air passes through the nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx and trachea. The trachea divides at the carina, at roughly the level of the sternal angle (about T4/T5). The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually enter the right side. The right lung has three lobes; the left has two (upper, with the lingula, and lower).
- Conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles): warms, humidifies and filters air but takes no part in gas exchange, so it forms the anatomical dead space (roughly 150 mL in an adult; approximate).
- Respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli): where gas exchange happens.
- Type I pneumocytes: thin, flat cells covering most of the alveolar surface, giving a very short diffusion distance.
- Type II pneumocytes: secrete surfactant and divide to replace type I cells.
- Alveolar macrophages: clear particles and microbes.

Visceral pleura covers each lung and parietal pleura lines the chest wall, with a thin film of fluid between them. The lungs tend to recoil inwards and the chest wall outwards, so intrapleural pressure is normally below atmospheric. If air enters the pleural space (pneumothorax) this coupling is lost and the lung collapses.
- Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure × volume is constant. Enlarging the thorax lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in.
- Quiet inspiration is active: the diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) contracts and flattens and the external intercostals raise the ribs.
- Quiet expiration is passive: the muscles relax and elastic recoil returns the lungs to resting volume. Forced breathing recruits accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid and scalenes in; internal intercostals and abdominal wall out).
- Compliance = ΔV ÷ ΔP. Fibrosis lowers it (stiff lungs); emphysema raises it (floppy lungs that recoil poorly).
- Surface tension tends to collapse alveoli. By Laplace (P = 2T/r) small alveoli would need higher pressure to stay open. Surfactant lowers surface tension, more so in small alveoli, stabilising them and reducing the work of breathing.

sections.h: Lung volumes and ventilation (approximate adult values)
sections.body:
- Tidal volume about 500 mL; total lung capacity about 6 L; residual volume about 1.2 L; vital capacity roughly 4.5–5 L.
- Functional residual capacity (FRC, the volume left after a quiet breath out) is about 2.4 L: the point where inward lung recoil balances outward chest-wall recoil.
- Spirometry only measures air that moves, so it cannot measure residual volume or FRC (these need methods such as gas dilution or body plethysmography).
- Minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate (0.5 L × 12 = 6 L/min).
- Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate ((500 − 150) mL × 12 = 4.2 L/min).
- Rapid shallow breathing wastes more of each breath: 250 mL × 24/min is still 6 L/min of minute ventilation, but alveolar ventilation is only (250 − 150) × 24 = 2.4 L/min.

A tall 20-year-old develops sudden one-sided chest pain and breathlessness. On that side breath sounds are reduced. The likely problem is a spontaneous pneumothorax: air in the pleural space abolishes the negative intrapleural pressure, so the lung's own elastic recoil collapses it while the chest wall springs slightly outwards.
The same principles explain other conditions. A baby born very preterm may lack surfactant, so small alveoli collapse and the work of breathing rises (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome). In pulmonary fibrosis low compliance means more pressure, and so more muscle work, is needed for each breath, and patients often breathe rapidly and shallowly. That pattern wastes a larger share of each breath on dead space, so more total ventilation is needed for the same alveolar ventilation.

- Students often think expiration always needs muscle work. In fact quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil; only forced expiration uses the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
- Students often think minute ventilation tells you how much air reaches the alveoli. It does not: dead space is ventilated on every breath, so the same minute ventilation can give very different alveolar ventilation.
- Students often think high compliance is always good. Emphysematous lungs are very compliant but recoil poorly, so air is trapped on expiration.
- Students often think the lungs are stuck to the chest wall. They are coupled by the pleural fluid film and the negative intrapleural pressure, which is why air in the pleural space lets the lung collapse.

notes.h: Gas exchange, gas transport and the control of breathing
notes.overview: Oxygen must diffuse into blood, be carried mostly on haemoglobin and be unloaded in tissues, while carbon dioxide travels back mainly as bicarbonate. Ventilation is set by chemoreceptors, chiefly responding to CO₂. The alveolar gas equation and A–a gradient tie these ideas to blood-gas results.
objectives: Apply Fick's law to explain how emphysema, fibrosis and altitude impair gas exchange.
Calculate alveolar PO₂ with the alveolar gas equation and use the A–a gradient to separate hypoventilation from gas-exchange problems.
Explain the shape of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve and the factors that shift it.
Describe the three forms of CO₂ carriage, the chloride shift and the Haldane effect.
Distinguish the roles of central and peripheral chemoreceptors.

sections.body:
- Fick's law: diffusion rate is proportional to area × diffusion constant × partial-pressure difference ÷ membrane thickness. Exchange falls if area falls (emphysema), thickness rises (fibrosis, pulmonary oedema) or the gradient falls (altitude). CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, so diffusion problems show first as low oxygen.
- Inspired PO₂ after humidification ≈ 0.21 × (101.3 − 6.3) ≈ 20 kPa (sea level, approximate).
- Alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = PIO₂ − PaCO₂/R, with R ≈ 0.8. So PAO₂ ≈ 20 − 5.3/0.8 = 20 − 6.6 ≈ 13.4 kPa (about 100 mmHg). Arterial PCO₂ is about 5.3 kPa (40 mmHg); 1 kPa ≈ 7.5 mmHg.
- Ventilation (V) must match perfusion (Q). Low V/Q (a blocked airway) acts like a shunt and causes hypoxaemia; high V/Q (a pulmonary embolus) behaves like dead space. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli.

sections.h: Carrying O₂ and CO₂, and controlling breathing
sections.body:
- About 98% of arterial O₂ is bound to haemoglobin (about 1.34 mL O₂ per gram). With Hb 150 g/L and saturation 98%: 1.34 × 150 × 0.98 ≈ 197 mL/L, plus about 3 mL/L dissolved ≈ 200 mL/L. Delivery = cardiac output × content ≈ 5 L/min × 200 mL/L ≈ 1,000 mL/min, against resting use of roughly 250 mL/min.
- The dissociation curve is sigmoid (cooperative binding). Its flat top protects saturation when alveolar PO₂ dips; its steep middle lets tissues unload much O₂ for a small fall in PO₂. Raised CO₂, H⁺ (Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG shift it right; fetal haemoglobin and carbon monoxide shift it left.
- CO₂ is carried about 70% as bicarbonate (carbonic anhydrase in red cells; HCO₃⁻ leaves in exchange for Cl⁻, the chloride shift), 20–25% as carbamino compounds and 5–10% dissolved (approximate). Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂ (Haldane effect).
- Medullary neurones generate the rhythm. Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H⁺, which tracks arterial PCO₂: the main minute-to-minute drive. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies via the glossopharyngeal nerve, aortic bodies via the vagus) respond to low PaO₂ (strongly below roughly 8 kPa), high PaCO₂ and high H⁺.

sections.h: Reading a blood gas: the A–a gradient
sections.body:
An arterial blood gas gives pH, PaO₂, PaCO₂ and bicarbonate. To ask why PaO₂ is low, compare it with the alveolar PO₂ predicted by the alveolar gas equation.
- A–a gradient = PAO₂ − PaO₂. On air it is typically below about 2 kPa in a young adult and rises with age (approximate).
- Raised PaCO₂ with a normal A–a gradient means pure hypoventilation (e.g. drug-induced respiratory depression, neuromuscular weakness): the lungs exchange gas normally but too little air is moved.
- A raised A–a gradient points to a gas-exchange problem: V/Q mismatch (the commonest), shunt or diffusion limitation.
Worked example on air: PaCO₂ 8.0 kPa, PaO₂ 9.0 kPa. PAO₂ = 20 − 8.0/0.8 = 10.0 kPa, so the gradient is 1.0 kPa: hypoventilation.

A person rescued from a house fire has a pulse-oximeter reading of 99% yet is confused and has a headache. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin far more avidly than O₂ and also shifts the curve left, so less O₂ is carried and what is carried is released less readily. Standard oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, so the saturation is falsely reassuring; co-oximetry on a blood gas measures it directly.
Contrast severe anaemia: saturation and PaO₂ are normal, but with Hb 85 g/L content is only about 1.34 × 85 × 0.98 + 3 ≈ 115 mL/L, so delivery falls unless cardiac output rises.

- Students often think a normal SpO₂ means oxygen delivery is fine. In fact delivery also depends on haemoglobin concentration and cardiac output, and oximetry can be misleading (carbon monoxide).
- Students often think low oxygen is the main stimulus to breathe. In healthy people CO₂ (via CSF H⁺) is the main drive; the hypoxic response becomes strong only when PaO₂ falls to roughly 8 kPa.
- Students often think 2,3-BPG increases oxygen binding. It binds deoxyhaemoglobin and lowers affinity, shifting the curve right.
- Students often think a raised PaCO₂ always means lung disease. With a normal A–a gradient it reflects hypoventilation from a cause outside the lungs.

notes.h: Structure of the heart, the cardiac cycle and its electrical activity
notes.overview: The heart is two pumps in series, driven by an electrical system that starts at the sinoatrial node and pauses at the atrioventricular node. Link each phase of the cardiac cycle to its valve events and heart sounds, each ion current to its action-potential phase, and each ECG wave to the event that produces it.
objectives: Describe the route of blood through the chambers, valves and great vessels.
Sequence the cardiac cycle with pressures, valve movements and heart sounds.
Explain the ionic basis of the ventricular and pacemaker action potentials.
Interpret basic ECG intervals and relate them to conduction through the heart.
Explain why the left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole.

sections.body:
- Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the superior and inferior venae cavae, crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and leaves through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
- Oxygenated blood returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle and leaves through the aortic valve into the aorta. The interventricular septum separates the ventricles.
- The left ventricular wall is much thicker because it generates far higher pressure: peak systolic pressure about 120 mmHg on the left and about 25 mmHg on the right (approximate).
- Coronary arteries arise just above the aortic valve. The left main stem divides into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries; the right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove. The left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, because contraction compresses its intramural vessels.

sections.h: Cardiac cycle, conduction and action potentials
sections.body:
- Cycle: atrial systole tops up ventricular filling; ventricular contraction raises pressure above atrial pressure and closes the atrioventricular valves (S1), starting isovolumetric contraction with all valves shut; ejection follows once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic and pulmonary pressure; isovolumetric relaxation begins as the semilunar valves close (S2); filling resumes, mostly passively, when the atrioventricular valves open. Valve opening is normally silent. S2 splits on inspiration because extra venous return to the right side delays pulmonary valve closure.
- Conduction: SA node (right atrium, near the SVC) → atria → AV node, which delays conduction (roughly 0.1 s) so the atria finish emptying → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
- Ventricular action potential: phase 0 fast Na⁺ influx; phase 1 transient K⁺ efflux; phase 2 plateau, L-type Ca²⁺ influx balancing K⁺ efflux; phase 3 K⁺ efflux; phase 4 stable resting potential. The long plateau gives a long refractory period, so the heart cannot be tetanised.
- Pacemaker cells drift upwards in phase 4 (the 'funny' current, mainly Na⁺ through HCN channels, then T-type Ca²⁺); L-type Ca²⁺ gives the upstroke. Noradrenaline (β1) steepens the slope; acetylcholine (M2) flattens it.
- Calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum lets Ca²⁺ bind troponin C so cross-bridges form.

- P wave: atrial depolarisation. PR interval: atria plus AV node (normally about 0.12–0.20 s, three to five small squares). QRS: ventricular depolarisation (normally under about 0.12 s). T wave: ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS.
- A PR interval longer than 0.20 s with every P wave followed by a QRS is first-degree heart block: a slowed but intact AV node.
- In complete (third-degree) heart block no atrial impulses reach the ventricles; P waves and QRS complexes march independently and a slow escape rhythm drives the ventricles.
- In atrial fibrillation there are no P waves and the R–R intervals are irregularly irregular.

An 80-year-old has dizzy spells. The ECG shows regular P waves at about 80 per minute and regular broad QRS complexes at about 38 per minute with no fixed relation between them. Conduction through the AV node has failed completely, so a slow ventricular escape pacemaker below the block has taken over. Because cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, the slow rate can lower blood pressure and cerebral perfusion. Compare a fit athlete with sinus rhythm at 48 per minute: every P wave conducts with a normal PR interval, and a large stroke volume maintains output.

- Students often think valve opening makes the heart sounds. In fact S1 and S2 come from valve closure; opening is normally silent.
- Students often think the T wave shows ventricular relaxation. It shows electrical repolarisation; mechanical relaxation follows it.
- Students often think the coronary arteries fill mainly in systole like other arteries. The left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, so a fast heart rate, which shortens diastole, reduces its supply time.
- Students often think the funny current is a K⁺ current. It is a mixed cation current carried mainly by Na⁺ through HCN channels.

- The left ventricular wall is much thicker because it generates far higher pressure: peak systolic pressure about 120 mmHg on the left and about 25 mmHg on the right (approximate).
- Coronary arteries arise just above the aortic valve. The left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, because contraction compresses its intramural vessels.

- Cycle: atrial systole tops up ventricular filling; ventricular contraction raises pressure above atrial pressure and closes the atrioventricular valves (S1), starting isovolumetric contraction with all valves shut; ejection follows once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic and pulmonary pressure; isovolumetric relaxation begins as the semilunar valves close (S2); filling resumes, mostly passively, when the atrioventricular valves open. Valve opening is normally silent. S2 splits on inspiration because extra venous return to the right side delays pulmonary valve closure.
- Conduction: SA node (right atrium, near the SVC) → atria → AV node, which delays conduction (roughly 0.1 s) so the atria finish emptying → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
- Ventricular action potential: phase 0 fast Na⁺ influx; phase 1 transient K⁺ efflux; phase 2 plateau, L-type Ca²⁺ influx balancing K⁺ efflux; phase 3 K⁺ efflux; phase 4 stable resting potential. The long plateau gives a long refractory period, so the heart cannot be tetanised.
- Pacemaker cells drift upwards in phase 4 (the 'funny' current, mainly Na⁺ through HCN channels, then T-type Ca²⁺); L-type Ca²⁺ gives the upstroke. Noradrenaline (β1) steepens the slope; acetylcholine (M2) flattens it.
- Calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum lets Ca²⁺ bind troponin C so cross-bridges form.

The ECG
- P wave: atrial depolarisation. PR interval: atria plus AV node (normally about 0.12–0.20 s, three to five small squares). QRS: ventricular depolarisation (normally under about 0.12 s). T wave: ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS.
- A PR interval longer than 0.20 s with every P wave followed by a QRS is first-degree heart block: a slowed but intact AV node.
- In complete (third-degree) heart block no atrial impulses reach the ventricles; P waves and QRS complexes march independently and a slow escape rhythm drives the ventricles.
- In atrial fibrillation there are no P waves and the R–R intervals are irregularly irregular.

Clinical application
An 80-year-old has dizzy spells. The ECG shows regular P waves at about 80 per minute and regular broad QRS complexes at about 38 per minute with no fixed relation between them. Conduction through the AV node has failed completely, so a slow ventricular escape pacemaker below the block has taken over. Because cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, the slow rate can lower blood pressure and cerebral perfusion. Compare a fit athlete with sinus rhythm at 48 per minute: every P wave conducts with a normal PR interval, and a large stroke volume maintains output.

- Students often think valve opening makes the heart sounds. In fact S1 and S2 come from valve closure; opening is normally silent.

- Students often think the coronary arteries fill mainly in systole like other arteries. The left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, so a fast heart rate, which shortens diastole, reduces its supply time.
- Students often think the funny current is a K⁺ current. It is a mixed cation current carried mainly by Na⁺ through HCN channels.

notes.h: Cardiac output, blood pressure and responses to changing demand
notes.overview: Two equations do most of the work: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, and mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × total peripheral resistance. Use them, with preload, afterload, contractility and the baroreceptor reflex, to reason step by step through posture, exercise and blood loss.
objectives: Calculate cardiac output, stroke volume, ejection fraction and mean arterial pressure from given values.
Explain how preload, afterload and contractility set stroke volume.
Apply Poiseuille's relationship to explain why arterioles control resistance.
Explain the baroreceptor response to standing and its failure in postural hypotension.
Explain oedema using Starling forces.

sections.body:
- Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate × stroke volume: about 70 beats/min × 70 mL ≈ 5 L/min at rest (approximate).
- Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume, e.g. 120 − 50 = 70 mL. Ejection fraction = SV ÷ EDV = 70 ÷ 120 ≈ 58% (normal above roughly 50–55%).
- Mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≈ CO × total peripheral resistance (TPR); strictly, the driving pressure is MAP minus central venous pressure. At rest MAP ≈ diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure: for 120/80, 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.
- Poiseuille: resistance ∝ viscosity × length ÷ radius⁴. Halving radius raises resistance 2⁴ = 16-fold. Arterioles are the main resistance vessels; veins are capacitance vessels holding roughly two-thirds of blood volume (approximate).
- Starling forces: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out; plasma oncotic pressure (mainly albumin) holds it in. Slightly more leaves than returns and lymphatics take back the excess. Oedema follows raised hydrostatic pressure (heart failure), low proteins (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), leaky capillaries (inflammation) or blocked lymphatics.

sections.h: Control of stroke volume and pressure
sections.body:
- Preload: end-diastolic stretch, set mainly by venous return. Frank–Starling: greater stretch gives stronger contraction, so output matches input.
- Afterload: the load against which the ventricle ejects, largely arterial pressure; higher afterload lowers stroke volume.
- Contractility: force at a given preload, raised by sympathetic β1 stimulation.
- Baroreflex: stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus) signal to the medulla. On standing, blood pools in leg veins, venous return and stroke volume fall and pressure dips; baroreceptor firing falls, so sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls. Heart rate, contractility, arteriolar tone and venous tone all rise, restoring pressure within seconds.
- Long-term control is renal: low renal perfusion releases renin, leading to angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, aldosterone, thirst) and sodium and water retention.
- Exercise: CO rises several-fold (roughly four to five times resting in a fit young adult; approximate). Local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine, low O₂) dilate muscle arterioles so TPR falls, while sympathetic constriction diverts flow from gut and skin. Systolic pressure rises and diastolic changes little or falls slightly.

A 75-year-old feels faint each time she stands. Lying BP is 142/80; after standing for one minute it is 112/68. Standing normally pools blood in the legs, and the baroreflex compensates within seconds. Here the systolic fall of 30 mmHg shows that compensation is inadequate: postural (orthostatic) hypotension. Possible reasons include autonomic dysfunction, volume depletion and blood-pressure-lowering medicines that blunt vasoconstriction or the heart-rate response. Reasoning with MAP ≈ CO × TPR tells you which limb (heart rate, stroke volume or resistance) is failing.

- Students often think MAP is the average of systolic and diastolic. At rest the heart spends longer in diastole, so MAP sits nearer diastolic (≈ diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure).
- Students often think resistance is inversely proportional to radius. It varies with 1/r⁴, so small changes in arteriolar radius have large effects on flow.
- Students often think TPR rises in exercise because of sympathetic activity. In fact metabolic vasodilation in muscle wins, and TPR falls.
- Students often think a raised stroke volume in exercise is due only to sympathetic drive. Increased venous return (muscle and respiratory pumps, venoconstriction) also raises preload via Frank–Starling.

notes.h: Origins and risk factors of common cardiovascular diseases
notes.overview: Atherosclerosis underlies most coronary disease and many strokes; hypertension both drives it and damages organs directly; heart failure is a common end-point. Learn how a plaque forms and why rupture, not narrowing alone, causes heart attacks, and how risk factors combine.
objectives: Describe the stages of atherosclerotic plaque formation and distinguish stable from unstable plaques.
Explain why plaque rupture causes acute coronary syndromes.
Distinguish modifiable from non-modifiable cardiovascular risk factors.
Apply NICE NG136 thresholds to classify a blood pressure result.
Explain how neurohormonal activation helps then harms in heart failure.

sections.body:
- Endothelial dysfunction is the starting point (hypertension, smoking, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, disturbed flow at branch points).
- LDL enters the intima and is oxidised. Monocytes enter and become macrophages, which take up oxidised LDL to become lipid-laden foam cells: the fatty streak, an early lesion.
- Smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and lay down collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich, necrotic core: the mature plaque.
- Stable plaques (thick caps) narrow the lumen gradually and cause symptoms on exertion (stable angina, intermittent claudication).
- Unstable plaques (thin caps, large lipid cores, many inflammatory cells) can rupture or erode. The exposed core activates platelets and a thrombus forms, causing an acute coronary syndrome or ischaemic stroke.

- Most adult hypertension is primary (essential), with no single identifiable cause; a minority is secondary (e.g. renal disease, primary hyperaldosteronism). Raised pressure damages endothelium and arterial walls and is a major risk factor for stroke, coronary disease, heart failure and kidney disease.
- Heart failure is a syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs at normal filling pressures. Common causes: ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, valve disease and cardiomyopathy.
- It is classified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) into reduced, mildly reduced and preserved types; the guideline thresholds are under Investigations.
- Falling output activates the sympathetic system and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. These support pressure at first but cause vasoconstriction, fluid retention and remodelling that worsen failure in the long run, which is why several heart-failure drugs block them.

- Non-modifiable: increasing age, male sex, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, ethnicity (for example, higher risk in people of South Asian family origin).
- Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, raised non-HDL (including LDL) cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, excess alcohol. Chronic kidney disease and some inflammatory conditions also raise risk. Risk factors multiply rather than simply add.
- Angina: chest pain from myocardial ischaemia when supply cannot meet demand. Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina and myocardial infarction) usually follows plaque rupture with thrombosis.
- Atrial fibrillation: stagnant atrial blood can clot and embolise, causing stroke.
- Venous thromboembolism: Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, vessel-wall injury) explains the risk factors (immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogen-containing medicines).

sections.h: Measuring risk, diagnosing hypertension and classifying heart failure
sections.body:
- QRISK3 estimates a person's 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke and is used in UK primary care to guide prevention (NICE NG238).
- NICE NG136: if clinic BP is 140/90 mmHg or higher, take a second reading (and a third if they differ substantially) and record the lower of the last two. Confirm with ambulatory monitoring (ABPM), or home monitoring (HBPM) if ABPM is unsuitable.
- Hypertension is diagnosed when clinic BP is 140/90 or more and the ABPM daytime or HBPM average is 135/85 or more.
- Stage 1: clinic 140/90 to 159/99 with an average of 135/85 to 149/94. Stage 2: clinic 160/100 or more (below 180/120) with an average of 150/95 or more. Severe: clinic systolic 180 or more, or diastolic 120 or more.
- Heart failure by LVEF: NICE NG106 (updated 2025) and the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guideline use the same bands: reduced, 40% or less; mildly reduced, 41–49%; preserved, 50% or more (NICE also requires supporting structural evidence for the preserved type).
Guidance changes: check the current NICE version.

A 52-year-old man of South Asian family origin who smokes and has type 2 diabetes notices tight central chest pain when walking uphill, easing within minutes of rest. His risk factors have promoted endothelial damage and plaque formation; a fixed, stable plaque limits flow so that supply fails only when demand rises (stable angina). If one day the pain comes at rest and does not settle, the likeliest explanation is rupture of a vulnerable plaque with thrombus: an acute coronary syndrome needing emergency assessment. Reducing his modifiable risks (stopping smoking, controlling pressure, lipids and glucose) slows plaque growth and lowers the chance of rupture.

- Students often think heart attacks come from the most severely narrowed arteries. Many follow rupture of plaques that caused little narrowing, because thin-capped lipid-rich plaques are the unstable ones.
- Students often think one high clinic reading means hypertension. NICE NG136 requires repeat clinic readings and confirmation with ambulatory or home monitoring.
- Students often think risk factors simply add up. They multiply, which is why combined-risk tools such as QRISK3 are used.
- Students often think heart failure means the heart has stopped. It means output is inadequate for the body's needs, often with preserved ejection fraction.

notes.h: Origins and risk factors of common respiratory diseases
notes.overview: Respiratory diseases are grouped first by their effect on airflow and lung volumes: obstructive (low FEV₁/FVC) or restrictive (low FVC, normal ratio). Learn the mechanisms of asthma and COPD, the risk factors for lung cancer, pneumonia and pulmonary embolism, and how lung disease can strain the heart.
objectives: Interpret spirometry as obstructive or restrictive using FEV₁, FVC and their ratio.
Distinguish asthma from COPD by cause, mechanism and reversibility.
Explain the emphysema patterns caused by smoking and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Calculate pack-years and apply CURB-65 components to a case.
Explain how chronic lung disease leads to cor pulmonale.

sections.body:
- Obstructive disease narrows airways so air cannot be blown out quickly: FEV₁ falls more than FVC and FEV₁/FVC is low (below 0.7 is the usual UK threshold for COPD in NICE guidance). Examples: asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis.
- Restrictive disease limits expansion: FVC is reduced and the ratio is normal or high. Examples: pulmonary fibrosis, chest-wall deformity, obesity, neuromuscular weakness.
- Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked: 20 a day for 40 years = 40 pack-years.
- Lung cancer: smoking is the dominant risk factor; others include radon, asbestos and air pollution. Main types are non-small-cell (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell) and small-cell.
- Pulmonary embolism usually comes from a leg deep-vein clot (Virchow's triad) and creates ventilated but unperfused lung (high V/Q).

- Asthma: chronic airway inflammation with variable airflow obstruction and airway hyper-responsiveness. Many cases are type 2 ('eosinophilic') inflammation: Th2 cytokines, IgE-mediated mast-cell activation, eosinophils, mucus hypersecretion and smooth-muscle contraction; airway remodelling can follow. Risk factors and triggers: atopy, family history, allergens, viral infections, cold air, exercise, smoke, occupational exposures, and some drugs (e.g. non-selective beta-blockers).
- COPD: persistent, progressive airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. Chronic bronchitis brings mucous gland hyperplasia and productive cough. Emphysema permanently enlarges airspaces by destroying alveolar walls; loss of elastic recoil and radial traction lets small airways collapse on expiration, trapping air.
- Smoking (the main UK cause) typically gives centriacinar emphysema, worst in the upper lobes. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leaves neutrophil elastase unchecked, giving panacinar emphysema, worst in the lower lobes, often in younger people. Occupational dusts and biomass smoke also cause COPD.
- Chronic hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale).

- Asthma symptoms (wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough) vary over time and are often worse at night or early morning.
- COPD: exertional breathlessness and chronic cough, often with sputum, in an older adult with significant smoking or other exposure.
- Community-acquired pneumonia is most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae; risk factors include older age, smoking, chronic lung disease and immunosuppression.
- CURB-65 helps judge pneumonia severity, one point each for: Confusion; Urea above 7 mmol/L; Respiratory rate 30/min or more; low Blood pressure (systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 mmHg or less); age 65 or over.
- Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) spreads by airborne droplets.

The joint 2024 guideline (NICE NG245 / SIGN 244) asks for objective tests, in sequence, in adults with a history suggesting asthma:
- First, a blood eosinophil count or FeNO (fractional exhaled nitric oxide): asthma is diagnosed if eosinophils are above the lab reference range or FeNO is 50 ppb or more.
- If not confirmed, spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility: an FEV₁ rise of 12% or more and 200 mL or more (or 10% or more of predicted) supports asthma.
- If spirometry is unavailable or delayed, twice-daily peak flow for 2 weeks: variability of 20% or more supports asthma.
- If asthma is still suspected but unconfirmed, refer for a bronchial challenge test.
For COPD, post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 confirms persistent obstruction. Guidance changes: check the current version.

A 64-year-old with 40 pack-years has worsening exertional breathlessness and a morning productive cough. Post-bronchodilator spirometry: FEV₁ 1.8 L (60% predicted), FVC 3.3 L, ratio 0.55. The ratio below 0.7 after a bronchodilator shows persistent obstruction, and with this history COPD is most likely. Compare a 22-year-old with eczema and night-time wheeze whose FeNO is raised: type 2 airway inflammation makes asthma likely, and her obstruction would be expected to vary and reverse.

- Students often think a low FVC always means restriction. FVC can fall in obstruction because air is trapped; check the ratio first.
- Students often think COPD and asthma are told apart by symptoms alone. Objective tests (and reversibility and variability) matter, and the two can coexist.
- Students often think emphysema in a young non-smoker must be due to passive smoking. Lower-lobe panacinar emphysema in a young person should prompt thought of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
- Students often think a pulmonary embolus causes low V/Q. It causes high V/Q (ventilated, unperfused lung), though hypoxaemia still occurs because blood is diverted to other areas, creating low V/Q there.

notes.h: Basic clinical skills and tests of cardiorespiratory function
notes.overview: Year 1 clinical skills are about measuring carefully and knowing what the numbers mean and how they can mislead: pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, peak flow, spirometry and the ECG. Follow the techniques you are taught in clinical skills sessions; this note explains the principles.
objectives: Explain how blood pressure is measured manually and the main sources of error.

notes.h: Principles of drug treatment for heart and lung disease
notes.overview: At Year 1 the focus is mechanism: which target each drug class acts on, what physiological change follows, and which adverse effect that mechanism predicts. This note gives no doses; in practice always use the BNF and current guidance.
objectives: Explain the mechanism of ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers and diuretics.
Explain how an adverse effect follows from a mechanism (for example ACE-inhibitor cough, hyperkalaemia).
Distinguish antiplatelet from anticoagulant drugs by target.
Explain how β2 agonists, muscarinic antagonists and inhaled corticosteroids improve airflow.
Apply the NICE step 1 hypertension choice and the 2024 asthma principles at a high level.

sections.body:
- ACE inhibitors (e.g. ramipril) block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II: vasodilation and less aldosterone, so less sodium and water retention. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, which accumulates, causing dry cough and, rarely, angioedema. Other effects: hyperkalaemia and changes in kidney function. Avoided in pregnancy.
- ARBs (e.g. losartan) block the AT1 receptor: similar benefits, little cough.
- Beta-blockers block cardiac β1 receptors, lowering heart rate and contractility (less myocardial O₂ demand) and renin release. Non-selective agents also block airway β2 receptors and can cause bronchospasm, so they are avoided in asthma.
- Calcium-channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) mainly dilate arterioles (ankle swelling is common); rate-limiting types (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow the heart and AV conduction.
- Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide) block the Na⁺/Cl⁻ co-transporter in the distal convoluted tubule; loop diuretics (furosemide) block Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ in the thick ascending limb and relieve fluid overload. Both can lower potassium.
- Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; liver cells make more LDL receptors and LDL falls. Muscle aches are a known effect.
- Nitrates release nitric oxide, mainly dilating veins and lowering preload, which relieves angina.

- Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1, reducing thromboxane A₂ for the platelet's lifetime (platelets cannot make new enzyme). P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel) block ADP-induced activation.
- Anticoagulants act on the clotting cascade: warfarin antagonises vitamin K; direct oral anticoagulants inhibit factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or thrombin (dabigatran). Used in atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism.
- Short-acting β2 agonists (salbutamol) raise cAMP in bronchial smooth muscle, causing relaxation; effects include tremor, tachycardia and low potassium. Long-acting agents (formoterol, salmeterol) last longer; formoterol also acts quickly.
- Muscarinic antagonists (ipratropium short-acting; tiotropium long-acting) block M3 receptors, preventing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction.
- Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation by changing gene transcription, treating the underlying inflammation in asthma. Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) block cysteinyl leukotriene receptors.

- Hypertension (NICE NG136): lifestyle advice first and throughout. Step 1 is an ACE inhibitor or ARB for people with type 2 diabetes (any age or family origin) and for people under 55 who are not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin. People aged 55 or over, and people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, without type 2 diabetes start with a calcium-channel blocker. For people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, NICE advises considering an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
- Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024): do not prescribe a short-acting β2 agonist without an inhaled corticosteroid. Newly diagnosed people aged 12 and over start with an as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol inhaler (AIR therapy), stepping up to maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) if not controlled; people who are highly symptomatic at diagnosis, or present with a severe exacerbation, start on MART.
These are principles, not prescribing instructions; check the current guidance and the BNF.

A 58-year-old with hypertension and no diabetes is started on a calcium-channel blocker; a few weeks later he notices ankle swelling. Arteriolar dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, so more fluid filters into the tissues (Starling forces): the swelling comes from the mechanism, not from heart failure. Another patient started on an ACE inhibitor develops a persistent dry cough; bradykinin accumulation explains it, and an ARB avoids it because it blocks the receptor without inhibiting ACE.

- Students often think aspirin is an anticoagulant. It is an antiplatelet drug; anticoagulants act on clotting factors.
- Students often think a SABA alone is a reasonable long-term asthma treatment. The 2024 guideline advises against SABA without an inhaled corticosteroid, because the reliever treats symptoms but not the inflammation.
- Students often think ARBs and ACE inhibitors have identical side effects. ARBs rarely cause cough, as they do not block bradykinin breakdown.
- Students often think nitrates relieve angina mainly by dilating coronary arteries. Their main effect is venodilation, which lowers preload and myocardial O₂ demand.

notes.overview: Clinical reasoning starts with a structured history, builds a differential ordered by likelihood and danger, and uses tests to shift probability. Learn sensitivity, specificity and predictive values, the ABCDE approach and NEWS2, and the thinking errors that lead to missed diagnoses.
objectives: Structure a history and use SOCRATES to characterise pain.
Build a differential diagnosis for chest pain or breathlessness, ordered by likelihood and danger.
Calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV from a 2 × 2 table and explain the effect of prevalence.
Apply the ABCDE approach in order of threat to life.
Recognise anchoring, premature closure and availability bias.

sections.body:
- Most diagnoses come from the history: presenting complaint, its history, past medical history, drugs and allergies, family history, social history (smoking and pack-years, alcohol, occupation) and systems review.
- For pain, SOCRATES: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Time course, Exacerbating and relieving factors, Severity.
- A differential is a list of possible causes ordered by likelihood and by how dangerous they would be to miss.
- Chest pain: cardiac (acute coronary syndrome, angina, pericarditis), respiratory (pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia), aortic (dissection), gastrointestinal (reflux) and musculoskeletal.
- Breathlessness: cardiac (heart failure, arrhythmia), respiratory (asthma, COPD, pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, fibrosis) and other (anaemia, anxiety, metabolic acidosis). Link symptoms to physiology: orthopnoea suggests raised pulmonary venous pressure in left heart failure.

- Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with the disease. A highly sensitive test, when negative, helps rule out ('SnNOut').
- Specificity = true negatives ÷ all without the disease. A highly specific test, when positive, helps rule in ('SpPIn').
- PPV = true positives ÷ all positives; it depends on prevalence (pre-test probability).
Worked example: sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%, 1,000 people, prevalence 10%. 100 have the disease: 90 true positives, 10 false negatives. 900 do not: 720 true negatives, 180 false positives. PPV = 90 ÷ 270 ≈ 33%; NPV = 720 ÷ 730 ≈ 98.6%.
With the same test at 50% prevalence, PPV rises to about 82% (450 ÷ 550). Tests help most when targeted at people with a reasonable pre-test probability.

sections.h: Recognising and responding to the unwell patient
sections.body:
- Resuscitation Council UK's ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) is used for any deteriorating patient: complete an initial assessment, treat life-threatening problems before moving on, reassess regularly and after each treatment, call for help early, use the whole team and hand over in a structured way (e.g. SBAR).
- NEWS2 (Royal College of Physicians, 2017) scores respiration rate, oxygen saturation, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, level of consciousness or new confusion, and temperature, and adds points for supplemental oxygen. Higher totals trigger more urgent review.
- Shared decisions: the GMC's guidance on decision making and consent (2020) expects doctors to discuss options, risks and benefits so the patient can choose.
Check the current Resuscitation Council UK, RCP and GMC versions.

A 30-year-old with known anxiety presents breathless and is labelled 'another panic attack'. She has recently had leg surgery and her heart rate is 112. Anchoring on the first label and premature closure would miss pulmonary embolism, which is dangerous and plausible after immobility. Asking 'what else could this be?', and putting dangerous diagnoses high on the list, protects against this. Her NEWS2 is raised by the tachycardia, prompting review rather than reassurance.

- Students often think a positive result on a good test means the patient almost certainly has the disease. With low prevalence most positives can be false (PPV 33% in the example).
- Students often think sensitivity and PPV are the same. Sensitivity is fixed by the test; PPV changes with prevalence.
- Students often think ABCDE means finishing the whole assessment before treating. Problems are treated as they are found, then the patient is reassessed.
- Students often think cognitive biases affect only inexperienced doctors. Everyone is prone to them; deliberate safeguards and senior input help.

cards.f: Anatomical dead space
cards.b: Volume of the conducting airways (nose to terminal bronchioles) where no gas exchange occurs; roughly 150 mL in an adult (approximate).
cards.ex: The conducting zone moves air but has no alveoli, so the air in it never takes part in exchange.

cards.f: Why do inhaled foreign bodies usually lodge in the right lung?
cards.b: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so it is the more direct path from the trachea.
cards.ex: Think of the angle at the carina: the right bronchus continues almost straight down.

cards.f: How does surfactant keep small alveoli open?
cards.b: It lowers surface tension, more so in small alveoli. By Laplace (P = 2T/r) this stops small alveoli emptying into large ones and reduces the work of breathing.
cards.ex: Without surfactant, a small radius means a high collapsing pressure; surfactant cuts T most where r is small.

cards.f: Why is quiet expiration passive?
cards.b: The inspiratory muscles relax and the elastic recoil of the lungs (plus surface tension) returns them to FRC, raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric.
cards.ex: No muscle is needed: the energy stored in stretched lung tissue during inspiration drives air out.

cards.f: Compliance in pulmonary fibrosis vs emphysema
cards.b: Fibrosis: compliance falls (stiff lungs, more pressure per litre). Emphysema: compliance rises (floppy lungs with poor elastic recoil, so air is trapped).
cards.ex: Compliance = ΔV/ΔP: stiff tissue gives a small ΔV for a given ΔP; destroyed elastic tissue gives a large one.

cards.f: Tidal volume 500 mL, dead space 150 mL, rate 12/min: alveolar ventilation?
cards.b: (500 − 150) mL × 12 = 4,200 mL/min = 4.2 L/min (minute ventilation would be 6.0 L/min).
cards.ex: Subtract dead space from each breath before multiplying by the rate.

cards.f: Why can simple spirometry not measure FRC or residual volume?
cards.b: Spirometry only records air that moves in or out; residual volume never leaves the lungs, and FRC includes it. Gas dilution or plethysmography is needed.
cards.ex: Any volume that contains residual volume (FRC, TLC) cannot be read off a spirometer trace.

cards.f: Sudden pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds on one side in a tall young man: what has happened to intrapleural pressure?
cards.b: Air has entered the pleural space (pneumothorax), so intrapleural pressure rises towards atmospheric and the lung recoils inwards and collapses.
cards.ex: The lung stays expanded only because intrapleural pressure is negative; lose that and recoil wins.

cards.f: PIO₂ 20 kPa, PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa, R 0.8: alveolar PO₂?
cards.b: PAO₂ = 20 − 5.3/0.8 = 20 − 6.6 ≈ 13.4 kPa (approximate).
cards.ex: Divide PaCO₂ by R before subtracting; forgetting R gives 14.7 kPa.

cards.f: Right shift vs left shift of the O₂–Hb curve
cards.b: Right (less affinity, more unloading): raised CO₂, H⁺, temperature, 2,3-BPG. Left (more affinity): the opposite changes, fetal Hb, carbon monoxide.
cards.ex: Right-shift conditions are those found in active muscle, which needs more O₂ unloaded.

cards.f: Why does the flat top of the dissociation curve matter?
cards.b: Saturation barely falls when alveolar PO₂ dips a little (e.g. mild altitude), so arterial O₂ content is protected.
cards.ex: On the plateau, large PO₂ changes give small saturation changes; the steep part is for unloading in tissues.

cards.f: The chloride shift
cards.b: In red cells carbonic anhydrase makes H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ from CO₂ and water; HCO₃⁻ leaves in exchange for Cl⁻ via an anion exchanger, keeping the cell neutral.
cards.ex: This is how most CO₂ (about 70%) ends up carried as plasma bicarbonate.

cards.f: On air: PaCO₂ 8.0 kPa, PaO₂ 9.0 kPa. A–a gradient and meaning?
cards.b: PAO₂ = 20 − 8.0/0.8 = 10.0 kPa; A–a = 10.0 − 9.0 = 1.0 kPa (normal). The low PaO₂ is due to hypoventilation, not a lung gas-exchange problem.
cards.ex: A raised PaCO₂ with a normal A–a gradient = hypoventilation (e.g. drug-induced respiratory depression).

cards.f: Central vs peripheral chemoreceptors
cards.b: Central (medulla): sense CSF H⁺, which tracks PaCO₂; main moment-to-moment drive. Peripheral (carotid via CN IX, aortic via CN X): low PaO₂, high PaCO₂, high H⁺.
cards.ex: Only the peripheral receptors respond to hypoxia, and strongly only below roughly 8 kPa.

cards.f: Why can SpO₂ read normal in carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.b: Standard oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ looks normal although O₂ content and unloading are reduced.
cards.ex: Co-oximetry on a blood gas measures carboxyhaemoglobin directly.

cards.f: Low V/Q vs high V/Q
cards.b: Low V/Q (perfused but poorly ventilated, e.g. blocked airway) acts like shunt and causes hypoxaemia. High V/Q (ventilated, poorly perfused, e.g. PE) acts like dead space.
cards.ex: Ask which is missing: air (low V/Q) or blood (high V/Q).

cards.f: Which valve closures produce S1 and S2?
cards.b: S1: mitral and tricuspid closure at the start of ventricular systole. S2: aortic and pulmonary closure at the start of ventricular relaxation.
cards.ex: Heart sounds come from valve closure; opening is normally silent.

cards.f: Why does S2 split on inspiration?
cards.b: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying pulmonary valve closure after aortic closure.
cards.ex: More right-sided filling → longer right ejection → later P2.

cards.f: Why does the AV node delay conduction?
cards.b: So the atria finish contracting and emptying before the ventricles contract; it also limits the ventricular rate if the atrial rate becomes very fast.
cards.ex: The delay (about 0.1 s) is visible as part of the PR interval.

cards.f: What maintains the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential?
cards.b: Inward L-type Ca²⁺ current balanced by outward K⁺ current; the long plateau gives a long refractory period that prevents tetany.
cards.ex: Na⁺ = phase 0 upstroke; Ca²⁺ = plateau; K⁺ = repolarisation.

cards.f: How does sympathetic stimulation raise heart rate?
cards.b: Noradrenaline on β1 receptors increases the funny (HCN) current and Ca²⁺ currents, steepening the phase 4 pacemaker slope so threshold is reached sooner.
cards.ex: Vagal acetylcholine (M2) does the opposite: flatter slope, slower rate.

cards.f: Why does tachycardia reduce left ventricular blood supply?
cards.b: The LV is perfused mainly in diastole (systole compresses its intramural vessels), and a faster heart rate shortens diastole most.
cards.ex: Rising heart rate cuts diastolic time much more than systolic time.

cards.f: Regular rhythm, P before every QRS, PR 7 small squares, QRS 2 small squares: interpretation?
cards.b: PR = 7 × 0.04 = 0.28 s (> 0.20 s) with every P conducted: first-degree heart block (AV nodal delay). QRS 0.08 s is normal.
cards.ex: One small square is 0.04 s at 25 mm/s; normal PR is 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares).

cards.f: First-degree vs complete heart block on the ECG
cards.b: First-degree: every P conducts, fixed long PR (> 0.20 s). Complete: no P waves conduct; P waves and QRS complexes are independent, with a slow escape rhythm.
cards.ex: Ask: does every P have its own QRS at a fixed interval?

cards.f: HR 80/min, EDV 130 mL, ESV 60 mL: SV, CO and EF?
cards.ex: EF uses stroke volume, not ESV, divided by EDV.

cards.f: Estimate MAP for a resting BP of 150/90 mmHg
cards.ex: Diastole lasts longer at rest, so add one-third of the pulse pressure to diastolic.

cards.f: Why does halving an arteriole's radius raise resistance 16-fold?
cards.b: Poiseuille: resistance ∝ viscosity × length / r⁴, so halving r multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16.
cards.ex: The fourth-power dependence is why arterioles are the main controllers of resistance.

cards.f: Frank–Starling mechanism
cards.b: Greater end-diastolic stretch (preload) increases the force of contraction, so stroke volume rises to match venous return.
cards.ex: It matches the outputs of the two ventricles beat by beat.

cards.f: Preload vs afterload
cards.b: Preload: ventricular stretch at the end of diastole (set mainly by venous return). Afterload: the load the ventricle ejects against (largely arterial pressure).
cards.ex: Preload raises stroke volume (Frank–Starling); afterload lowers it.

cards.f: Baroreflex on standing up
cards.b: Venous pooling → SV and BP fall → less carotid sinus/aortic arch stretch → less firing (CN IX, X) → more sympathetic, less vagal → HR, contractility, TPR and venous tone rise.
cards.ex: Reason with MAP ≈ CO × TPR: each limb is pushed back up.

cards.f: Why does TPR fall during exercise?
cards.b: Local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine, low O₂) dilate arterioles in working muscle, outweighing sympathetic constriction elsewhere.
cards.ex: Systolic pressure still rises because cardiac output rises more than TPR falls.

cards.f: Lying BP 142/80, standing (after 1 min) 112/68, with faintness: interpretation?
cards.b: A 30 mmHg systolic fall on standing: postural (orthostatic) hypotension, meaning the baroreflex response is inadequate.
cards.ex: Think autonomic dysfunction, volume depletion or medicines that blunt the reflex.

cards.f: How does a foam cell form?
cards.b: Monocytes enter the intima, become macrophages and engulf oxidised LDL, becoming lipid-laden foam cells; collections form the fatty streak.
cards.ex: Endothelial cells let LDL and monocytes in but do not themselves become foam cells.

cards.f: Stable vs unstable plaque
cards.b: Stable: thick fibrous cap, small lipid core, gradual narrowing, exertional symptoms. Unstable: thin cap, large lipid core, inflammation; prone to rupture and thrombosis.
cards.ex: Cap thickness and inflammation, not degree of narrowing, decide rupture risk.

cards.f: Why can a plaque causing little narrowing still cause a sudden MI?
cards.b: If its thin cap ruptures, the thrombogenic core is exposed; platelets aggregate and a thrombus forms that can suddenly occlude the artery.
cards.ex: The thrombus, not the original plaque size, blocks the vessel.

cards.f: Clinic BP 152/94 (repeated), daytime ABPM 141/88: NICE NG136 category?
cards.b: Stage 1 hypertension: clinic 140/90 to 159/99 and ABPM/HBPM average 135/85 to 149/94.
cards.ex: Use 135/85 (not 140/90) as the threshold for ambulatory or home averages.

cards.f: Immobile for 3 days after hip surgery, now a swollen calf: which parts of Virchow's triad?
cards.b: Stasis (immobility) plus hypercoagulability and vessel-wall injury after surgery: all three elements contribute to DVT.
cards.ex: Virchow's triad: stasis, hypercoagulability, vessel-wall injury.

cards.f: Why does neurohormonal activation worsen heart failure in the long run?
cards.b: Sympathetic and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation support pressure at first but cause vasoconstriction (higher afterload), fluid retention and remodelling.
cards.ex: This is why several heart-failure drugs block these systems.

cards.f: Non-modifiable cardiovascular risk factors
cards.b: Increasing age, male sex, family history of premature CVD, ethnicity (e.g. higher risk with South Asian family origin).
cards.ex: Modifiable factors include smoking, BP, non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity and inactivity.

cards.f: QRISK3
cards.b: A tool used in UK primary care to estimate a person's 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke, guiding prevention (NICE NG238).
cards.ex: It combines many risk factors because they multiply rather than add.

cards.f: FEV₁ 1.5 L, FVC 3.0 L: pattern?
cards.b: FEV₁/FVC = 0.5 (< 0.7): obstructive. FVC can also be low in obstruction because of air trapping.
cards.ex: Always calculate the ratio before judging FVC.

cards.f: Emphysema in smokers vs alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
cards.b: Smoking: centriacinar, upper lobes. A1AT deficiency: panacinar, lower lobes, often younger patients (unopposed neutrophil elastase).
cards.ex: Young, lower-lobe, panacinar → think A1AT deficiency.

cards.f: 30 cigarettes a day for 30 years: pack-years?
cards.ex: One pack-year = 20 cigarettes a day for one year.

cards.f: Pneumonia, aged 72, new confusion, urea 9 mmol/L, RR 32/min, BP 104/64: CURB-65?
cards.b: Confusion 1, urea > 7: 1, RR ≥ 30: 1, BP 0 (systolic not < 90, diastolic not ≤ 60), age ≥ 65: 1 → score 4.
cards.ex: BP scores only if systolic < 90 or diastolic ≤ 60.

cards.f: Asthma vs COPD: obstruction
cards.b: Asthma: variable, largely reversible obstruction from airway inflammation and hyper-responsiveness. COPD: persistent, progressive, not fully reversible.
cards.ex: Variability and reversibility point to asthma; persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction to COPD.

cards.f: Why do small airways collapse on expiration in emphysema?
cards.b: Destroyed alveolar walls remove elastic recoil and the radial traction that holds small airways open, so they close early and trap air.
cards.ex: This lowers FEV₁ much more than FVC and causes hyperinflation.

cards.f: How does chronic lung disease cause cor pulmonale?
cards.b: Chronic alveolar hypoxia → hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → right ventricular strain and failure.
cards.ex: Cor pulmonale is right heart failure caused by lung disease.

cards.f: First objective tests for asthma in adults (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024)
cards.b: Blood eosinophil count or FeNO: asthma if eosinophils above the lab range or FeNO ≥ 50 ppb; then bronchodilator reversibility, PEF variability, bronchial challenge.
cards.ex: Guidance as checked in October 2026; check the current version.

cards.f: Korotkoff sounds for blood pressure
cards.b: Phase I (first sound) = systolic pressure; phase V (disappearance of sounds) = diastolic pressure.
cards.ex: Deflate slowly so you do not miss the first sound.

cards.f: Why does too small a BP cuff overestimate pressure?
cards.b: A narrow bladder needs more cuff pressure to compress the brachial artery, so the reading is falsely high (too large a cuff tends to underestimate).
cards.ex: Match the bladder to the arm circumference.

cards.f: Lying 130/80, standing (1 min) 106/76: significant postural drop?
cards.b: Yes: systolic fall of 24 mmHg (≥ 20 mmHg is significant in NICE NG136); diastolic fall 4 mmHg.
cards.ex: Significant = systolic fall ≥ 20 or diastolic fall ≥ 10 mmHg after standing at least 1 minute.

cards.f: How does a pulse oximeter estimate SpO₂?
cards.b: From the different absorption of red and infrared light by oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin, using the pulsatile (arterial) part of the signal.
cards.ex: It cannot detect CO₂ and is fooled by carboxyhaemoglobin.

cards.f: Peak flow vs spirometry
cards.b: PEF: fastest flow in a forced breath out; cheap, good for tracking variability. Spirometry: FEV₁, FVC and ratio; defines obstructive vs restrictive patterns.
cards.ex: PEF is effort-dependent and gives no FVC, so it cannot show restriction.

cards.f: Regular rhythm, 20 small squares between R waves: heart rate?
cards.ex: 1,500 ÷ small squares or 300 ÷ large squares, regular rhythms only.

cards.f: Irregularly irregular strip, 18 QRS complexes in 10 s: rate?
cards.b: 18 × 6 = 108 beats/min.
cards.ex: For irregular rhythms, count over 10 seconds and multiply by 6.

cards.f: Acutely unwell COPD patient at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure: target SpO₂ (BTS)?
cards.b: 88–92% (94–98% for most other acutely ill adults). BTS 2017 guideline, current as checked October 2026.
cards.ex: Excess oxygen can worsen CO₂ retention in susceptible patients.

cards.f: Why do ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough?
cards.b: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; inhibiting it lets bradykinin accumulate in the airways.
cards.ex: ARBs block the AT1 receptor without affecting bradykinin, so cough is rare.

cards.f: Why can ACE inhibitors raise potassium?
cards.b: Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, so the kidney excretes less K⁺.
cards.ex: Aldosterone normally promotes Na⁺ retention and K⁺ excretion in the distal nephron.

cards.f: Aspirin vs anticoagulants
cards.b: Aspirin: antiplatelet, irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 (less thromboxane A₂). Anticoagulants: act on clotting factors (warfarin via vitamin K; DOACs on factor Xa or thrombin).
cards.ex: Antiplatelets stop platelet aggregation; anticoagulants stop fibrin formation.

cards.f: How does salbutamol relieve bronchospasm?
cards.b: β2 agonist: raises cAMP in bronchial smooth muscle, causing relaxation. Effects include tremor, tachycardia and low potassium.
cards.ex: M3 blockade is how ipratropium and tiotropium work.

cards.f: 62-year-old, no diabetes, confirmed hypertension: NICE step 1 class?
cards.b: A calcium-channel blocker (aged 55 or over without type 2 diabetes), alongside lifestyle advice (NG136).
cards.ex: ACE inhibitor or ARB is step 1 for type 2 diabetes or under 55 (not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin).

cards.f: Newly diagnosed adult asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024): first treatment approach?
cards.b: As-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR therapy), or MART from the start if highly symptomatic; step up to MART if not controlled. SABA without ICS is not recommended.
cards.ex: Every step includes an inhaled corticosteroid to treat the inflammation.

cards.f: Why do dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers cause ankle swelling?
cards.b: Arteriolar dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, so more fluid filters into the tissues (Starling forces).
cards.ex: The oedema is a vascular effect, not a sign of heart failure.

cards.f: Loop vs thiazide diuretic site of action
cards.b: Loop: Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter, thick ascending limb. Thiazide: Na⁺/Cl⁻ co-transporter, distal convoluted tubule. Both can lower potassium.
cards.ex: Loop diuretics are more powerful and relieve fluid overload in heart failure.

cards.f: Sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%, prevalence 10%: PPV?
cards.ex: Build the 2 × 2 table from prevalence first.

cards.f: Sensitivity vs positive predictive value
cards.b: Sensitivity: TP ÷ all with disease (a property of the test). PPV: TP ÷ all positive results (changes with prevalence).
cards.ex: Lower prevalence → more false positives → lower PPV, sensitivity unchanged.

cards.f: Why does a negative result on a highly sensitive test help rule out disease?
cards.b: A highly sensitive test rarely misses disease (few false negatives), so a negative result makes disease unlikely (SnNOut), unless pre-test probability is high.
cards.ex: Specific test + positive result helps rule in (SpPIn).

cards.f: Stridor, SpO₂ 88%, HR 120, BP 92/58: what comes first in ABCDE?
cards.b: The airway: treat airway obstruction before moving on to breathing and circulation, then reassess.
cards.ex: ABCDE tackles problems in order of threat to life; treat as you find.

cards.f: NEWS2 parameters
cards.b: Respiration rate, SpO₂, systolic BP, pulse rate, consciousness or new confusion, temperature, plus extra points for supplemental oxygen.
cards.ex: Capillary refill time is part of ABCDE but not scored in NEWS2.

cards.f: Breathless patient with anxiety, recent leg surgery and HR 112 labelled 'panic attack': which error?
cards.b: Anchoring and premature closure: sticking to the first label despite features suggesting a dangerous alternative (pulmonary embolism).
cards.ex: Ask 'what else could this be?' and put dangerous diagnoses high on the list.

cards.f: SOCRATES
cards.b: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity.
cards.ex: A structure for characterising pain in the history.

cards.f: Why does orthopnoea suggest left heart failure?
cards.b: Lying flat increases venous return; a failing left ventricle cannot handle it, so pulmonary venous pressure rises and fluid enters the lungs.
cards.ex: Link the symptom to the physiology rather than memorising it.

questions.q: A person breathes with a tidal volume of 500 mL at 12 breaths per minute. Anatomical dead space is 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
options: 7.8 L/min
6.0 L/min
1.8 L/min
4.2 L/min
questions.why: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate = (500 − 150) × 12 = 4,200 mL/min = 4.2 L/min. Only the part of each breath that passes beyond the conducting airways reaches the alveoli.
optWhy: This is minute ventilation (500 × 12); it forgets to remove the dead space from each breath.
This is dead-space ventilation (150 × 12), the part of each minute's ventilation that never reaches the alveoli.
Correct: (500 − 150) mL × 12 = 4,200 mL/min.
This adds dead space to tidal volume ((500 + 150) × 12) instead of subtracting it.
questions.clue: Tidal volume 500 mL, rate 12/min and dead space 150 mL are all given.
questions.concept: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate.

followUp.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis breathes rapidly and shallowly: tidal volume 250 mL at 24 breaths per minute, dead space 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
options: 2.4 L/min
6.0 L/min
3.6 L/min
9.6 L/min
followUp.why: (250 − 150) × 24 = 2,400 mL/min = 2.4 L/min. 6.0 L/min is the minute ventilation (250 × 24), the same as in a normal 500 mL × 12 pattern, which shows why minute ventilation can mislead. 3.6 L/min is the dead-space ventilation (150 × 24). 9.6 L/min adds dead space to tidal volume ((250 + 150) × 24).

questions.q: Which cells in the alveolar wall secrete surfactant?
options: Goblet cells
Alveolar macrophages
Type II pneumocytes
Type I pneumocytes
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, which lowers alveolar surface tension, and act as progenitors for type I cells. Type I cells are the ones most often confused with them because both line the alveolus.
optWhy: Type I pneumocytes are the thin, flat cells forming most of the gas-exchange surface; they do not secrete surfactant.
Goblet cells secrete mucus in the conducting airways, not surfactant in the alveoli.
Alveolar macrophages are defensive cells that clear particles and microbes.
Correct: type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and can divide to replace type I cells.
questions.concept: Cell types of the alveolus and their functions.

followUp.q: A baby born at 28 weeks' gestation develops grunting, rib recession and a rapidly rising work of breathing. Lack of which product best explains this?
options: Mucus from goblet cells
Surfactant from type II pneumocytes
Elastin from fibroblasts
Lysozyme from alveolar macrophages
followUp.why: Very preterm babies may not yet make enough surfactant, so surface tension collapses small alveoli (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome) and each breath needs more work. Mucus, elastin and lysozyme are real airway products but their lack does not cause this picture.

questions.q: A tall 19-year-old develops sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness at rest. Breath sounds are reduced over the right lung. Which change best explains why his right lung has collapsed?
options: The right phrenic nerve has failed, so the diaphragm cannot expand the lung
Lung compliance has risen sharply, so the lung cannot hold its volume
Surfactant production has stopped, so surface tension has collapsed the lung
Air in the pleural space has abolished the negative intrapleural pressure, so the lung recoils inwards
questions.why: The lung tends to recoil inwards and the chest wall outwards; the pleural fluid film and negative intrapleural pressure couple them. Air entering the pleural space (a spontaneous pneumothorax, typical in tall young men) breaks the coupling and the lung collapses under its own recoil.
optWhy: Surfactant loss would affect both lungs gradually and is a problem of preterm babies or severe lung injury, not sudden one-sided collapse.
Correct: with air in the pleural space the lung is no longer held out by negative intrapleural pressure, and its elastic recoil collapses it (pneumothorax).
Phrenic nerve failure paralyses the hemidiaphragm and reduces expansion, but it does not cause sudden pleuritic pain or collapse of the lung away from the chest wall.
Rising compliance (as in emphysema) makes lungs easier to inflate; it does not cause sudden collapse.
questions.clue: Sudden one-sided pleuritic pain with reduced breath sounds in a tall young man.
questions.concept: Negative intrapleural pressure couples the lung to the chest wall.

followUp.q: Why does the chest wall on the side of a large pneumothorax tend to spring slightly outwards?
options: Pleural pressure is always far above atmospheric in any pneumothorax
The intercostal muscles go into sustained spasm
Surfactant leaks out and stiffens the chest wall
Its natural outward recoil is no longer opposed by the inward pull of the lung
followUp.why: At FRC the outward recoil of the chest wall balances the inward recoil of the lung. Once the pleural coupling is lost, each moves towards its own resting position: the lung collapses inwards and the chest wall springs out. Pressure far above atmospheric occurs only in tension pneumothorax, not in every case; muscle spasm and surfactant are not involved.

questions.q: Explain how air is drawn into the lungs during quiet inspiration and why quiet expiration is normally passive.
markScheme: Diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) contracts and flattens; external intercostals raise the ribs, increasing thoracic volume
Pleural coupling means lung volume increases with the chest wall; intrapleural pressure becomes more negative
Boyle's law: rising alveolar volume lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in down the pressure gradient
In quiet expiration the muscles relax and elastic recoil of the lungs (and surface tension) returns them to FRC
Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric so air flows out without active muscle contraction
questions.modelAnswer: During quiet inspiration the diaphragm, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), contracts and moves down, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs. Thoracic volume increases. Because the visceral and parietal pleura are held together by the thin pleural fluid layer, the lungs expand with the chest wall and intrapleural pressure becomes more negative. By Boyle's law, the rise in alveolar volume lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in until the pressures equalise. In quiet expiration the inspiratory muscles simply relax. The elastic tissue of the lungs and the surface tension of the alveolar lining make the lungs recoil, alveolar volume falls, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric and air flows out. No muscle contraction is needed, so quiet expiration is passive; forced expiration adds the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
questions.concept: Boyle's law, pleural coupling and elastic recoil drive ventilation.

questions.q: Which change increases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the left?
options: A rise in red-cell 2,3-BPG
A fall in plasma pH
A fall in blood temperature
A rise in arterial PCO₂
questions.why: Cooling raises affinity, so a fall in temperature shifts the curve left. Raised CO₂, H⁺ (lower pH) and 2,3-BPG all lower affinity and shift it right, which is why active, warm, acidic muscle unloads more oxygen. 2,3-BPG can sound as if 'more binding' means more oxygen held, but it binds deoxyhaemoglobin and does the opposite.
optWhy: Correct: cooling raises haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and shifts the curve left.
A rise in PCO₂ shifts the curve right (partly through the Bohr effect), helping unloading in active tissue.
2,3-BPG binds and stabilises deoxyhaemoglobin, lowering affinity and shifting the curve right.
A fall in pH (more H⁺) shifts the curve right: the Bohr effect.
questions.concept: Factors that shift the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve.

followUp.q: Which change would shift the dissociation curve to the right in exercising muscle, increasing oxygen unloading?
options: A rise in carboxyhaemoglobin
A higher proportion of fetal haemoglobin
A rise in local temperature and PCO₂
A fall in red-cell 2,3-BPG
followUp.why: Working muscle is warmer and produces CO₂ and H⁺, all of which lower haemoglobin's affinity and shift the curve right. Carboxyhaemoglobin, fetal haemoglobin and a fall in 2,3-BPG all shift the curve left, holding oxygen more tightly.

questions.q: Inspired PO₂ (after humidification) is 20 kPa, arterial PCO₂ is 5.3 kPa and the respiratory quotient is 0.8. Using the alveolar gas equation, what is the alveolar PO₂?
options: About 26.6 kPa
About 13.4 kPa
About 14.7 kPa
About 6.6 kPa
questions.why: PAO₂ = PIO₂ − PaCO₂/R = 20 − 5.3/0.8 = 20 − 6.6 ≈ 13.4 kPa (about 100 mmHg). CO₂ entering the alveoli displaces oxygen, and dividing by R allows for more O₂ being taken up than CO₂ is added.
optWhy: This subtracts PaCO₂ without dividing by R (20 − 5.3).
This is only the CO₂ term (5.3/0.8), forgetting to subtract it from PIO₂.
This adds the CO₂ term instead of subtracting it (20 + 6.6).
questions.clue: PIO₂ 20 kPa, PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa and R 0.8 are given.
questions.concept: Alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = PIO₂ − PaCO₂/R.

followUp.q: At altitude a climber's inspired PO₂ is 13 kPa and hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ to 4.0 kPa (R 0.8). What is the alveolar PO₂?
options: About 9.0 kPa
About 8.0 kPa
About 18.0 kPa
About 5.0 kPa
followUp.why: PAO₂ = 13 − 4.0/0.8 = 13 − 5.0 = 8.0 kPa. 9.0 kPa forgets to divide by R (13 − 4.0); 18.0 kPa adds the CO₂ term; 5.0 kPa is the CO₂ term alone. Hyperventilation helps at altitude because a lower PaCO₂ makes room for more alveolar oxygen.

questions.q: A 45-year-old is drowsy after taking an opioid. Arterial blood gas on air: PaCO₂ 8.0 kPa, PaO₂ 9.0 kPa. Taking PIO₂ as 20 kPa and R as 0.8, what best explains the low PaO₂?
options: Diffusion impairment, because PaO₂ is below 10 kPa
V/Q mismatch, because the A–a gradient is raised (about 3 kPa)
Shunt, because the A–a gradient is raised (about 11 kPa)
Hypoventilation, because the A–a gradient is normal (about 1 kPa)
questions.why: PAO₂ = 20 − 8.0/0.8 = 10.0 kPa and PaO₂ is 9.0 kPa, so the A–a gradient is about 1 kPa: normal. A raised PaCO₂ with a normal gradient means hypoventilation, here from opioid depression of the respiratory centre. V/Q mismatch, shunt and diffusion problems all widen the gradient.
optWhy: About 3 kPa comes from forgetting to divide PaCO₂ by R (20 − 8.0 − 9.0); the true gradient is normal.
About 11 kPa comes from ignoring the CO₂ term altogether (20 − 9.0); it is not the A–a gradient.
Correct: PAO₂ = 20 − 8.0/0.8 = 10.0 kPa, so A–a = 10.0 − 9.0 = 1.0 kPa, which is normal; the lungs exchange gas normally but too little air is moved.
A low PaO₂ alone cannot identify the cause; diffusion impairment would raise the A–a gradient, and the high PaCO₂ points to reduced ventilation.
questions.clue: Raised PaCO₂ after an opioid, with values allowing the A–a gradient to be calculated.
questions.concept: A normal A–a gradient with high PaCO₂ indicates hypoventilation; a raised gradient indicates a gas-exchange problem.

followUp.q: Breathing air, a patient with pneumonia has PaCO₂ 4.0 kPa and PaO₂ 8.5 kPa (PIO₂ 20 kPa, R 0.8). What is the A–a gradient and what does it suggest?
options: About 6.5 kPa: raised, pointing to a gas-exchange problem such as V/Q mismatch
About 1.0 kPa: normal, so the cause is hypoventilation
About 11.5 kPa: raised, so the cause must be a large anatomical shunt
About 7.5 kPa: raised, so the cause must be diffusion limitation alone
followUp.why: PAO₂ = 20 − 4.0/0.8 = 15.0 kPa; A–a = 15.0 − 8.5 = 6.5 kPa, clearly raised. In pneumonia, perfused but poorly ventilated alveoli (low V/Q) are the main cause. 11.5 kPa ignores the CO₂ term (20 − 8.5) and 7.5 kPa forgets to divide by R (20 − 4.0 − 8.5); neither is the correct gradient, and a raised gradient alone cannot pin the cause on shunt or diffusion. The low PaCO₂ rules out hypoventilation.

questions.q: Describe how carbon dioxide is carried in the blood, giving approximate proportions, and explain the chloride shift.
markScheme: About 70% as bicarbonate (accept 60–70%)
Carbonic anhydrase in red cells catalyses CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; H⁺ buffered by haemoglobin
Chloride shift: HCO₃⁻ leaves red cell in exchange for Cl⁻ via an anion exchanger, maintaining electrical neutrality
About 20–25% as carbamino compounds (mostly with haemoglobin)
About 5–10% dissolved in plasma; Haldane effect increases carriage by deoxygenated blood
questions.modelAnswer: Most carbon dioxide, roughly 70%, is carried as bicarbonate. CO₂ diffuses into red cells, where carbonic anhydrase speeds its reaction with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. The H⁺ is buffered by haemoglobin. Bicarbonate moves out of the red cell into plasma in exchange for chloride through an anion-exchange protein; this is the chloride (Hamburger) shift, which keeps the cell electrically neutral. Around 20–25% of CO₂ binds to amino groups on proteins, mainly haemoglobin, as carbamino compounds, and about 5–10% is dissolved. These figures are approximate. Deoxygenated haemoglobin binds more CO₂ and H⁺ (the Haldane effect), so venous blood carries more CO₂ and releases it in the lungs when haemoglobin is oxygenated.
questions.concept: CO₂ transport as bicarbonate, carbamino compounds and dissolved gas.

questions.q: Which ionic current mainly maintains the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular myocyte action potential?
options: Inward L-type Ca²⁺ current
The pacemaker 'funny' current
Fast inward Na⁺ current
Outward delayed-rectifier K⁺ current
questions.why: The plateau is held by inward Ca²⁺ through L-type channels balanced against K⁺ efflux. It gives a long refractory period so the heart cannot be tetanised, and the Ca²⁺ entering triggers calcium-induced calcium release for contraction.
optWhy: The fast Na⁺ current causes the rapid upstroke in phase 0, not the plateau.
The delayed-rectifier K⁺ current dominates phase 3, when the cell repolarises.
Correct: Ca²⁺ entering through L-type channels balances K⁺ efflux and holds the membrane depolarised.
The funny current drives the slow phase 4 depolarisation of pacemaker cells, not the ventricular plateau.
