questions.concept: Ionic basis of the ventricular action potential.

followUp.q: A drug blocks L-type Ca²⁺ channels in ventricular muscle. Which effect would you expect?
options: A shorter, lower plateau and weaker contraction
A slower phase 0 upstroke and slower conduction through the ventricles
Loss of the phase 4 pacemaker drift in ventricular muscle cells
A longer phase 3 and a prolonged QT interval
followUp.why: Less Ca²⁺ entry shortens and lowers the plateau and reduces calcium-induced calcium release, so contraction weakens. A slower phase 0 would come from blocking fast Na⁺ channels. Ventricular muscle cells have a stable phase 4, so there is no drift to lose. A prolonged phase 3 would come from blocking K⁺ channels.

questions.q: Which event produces the first heart sound?
options: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Opening of the mitral and tricuspid valves
questions.why: The first heart sound occurs as the mitral and tricuspid valves close when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure at the start of systole. Students sometimes assume any valve movement makes a sound, but opening is silent.
optWhy: Opening of the atrioventricular valves is normally silent.
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves produces the second heart sound.
Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole is associated with a third heart sound, not the first.
Correct: S1 is produced as the atrioventricular valves close at the start of ventricular systole.
questions.concept: Heart sounds come from valve closure at defined points in the cycle.

followUp.q: During which phase of the cardiac cycle are all four valves closed while ventricular pressure rises?
options: Rapid ejection
Isovolumetric contraction
Isovolumetric relaxation
Atrial systole
followUp.why: After the atrioventricular valves close (S1) and before the semilunar valves open, the ventricles contract with no change in volume: isovolumetric contraction. In isovolumetric relaxation all valves are also shut, but pressure is falling. During ejection the semilunar valves are open, and in atrial systole the atrioventricular valves are open.

questions.q: A 70-year-old's ECG, recorded at 25 mm/s, shows a regular rhythm at 60 beats/min with a P wave before every QRS. The PR interval is 7 small squares and the QRS is 2 small squares wide. Which description fits best?
options: Normal sinus rhythm: the PR interval is within the normal range
First-degree heart block: PR 0.28 s from delayed AV nodal conduction
Complete heart block: the PR interval is long
Bundle branch block: conduction through the ventricles is slowed
questions.why: At 25 mm/s each small square is 0.04 s, so the PR interval is 0.28 s. A prolonged PR with every P conducted is first-degree heart block: the AV node is slow but every impulse gets through. The QRS (0.08 s) is normal.
optWhy: The normal PR is 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares); 7 small squares is too long.
Correct: 7 × 0.04 s = 0.28 s, above 0.20 s, with every P wave conducted.
In complete heart block P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated; here every P is followed by a QRS at a fixed interval.
The QRS is 2 × 0.04 = 0.08 s, which is narrow; bundle branch block widens the QRS to 0.12 s or more.
questions.clue: PR interval of 7 small squares with a P wave before every QRS.
questions.concept: Measuring ECG intervals and relating them to conduction through the AV node.

followUp.q: An ECG shows regular P waves at 80/min and regular broad QRS complexes at 38/min, with no consistent relationship between them. What is the rhythm?
options: First-degree heart block
Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response
Sinus bradycardia
Complete (third-degree) heart block with a ventricular escape rhythm
followUp.why: P waves and QRS complexes march independently, so no atrial impulses are reaching the ventricles; a slow, broad escape rhythm below the block drives them. In first-degree block every P is conducted with a fixed PR. Atrial fibrillation has no organised P waves and an irregular ventricular rhythm. In sinus bradycardia every P wave is followed by a QRS.

questions.q: On auscultation, a healthy 20-year-old has a second heart sound that splits into two components on inspiration and becomes single on expiration. What best explains this?
options: A septal defect lets blood cross between the ventricles on inspiration
Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, delaying pulmonary valve closure
Inspiration increases left ventricular filling, delaying aortic valve closure
The mitral and tricuspid valves close at different times during inspiration
questions.why: Falling intrathoracic pressure in inspiration draws more blood into the right heart. Right ventricular ejection lasts longer and the pulmonary valve closes after the aortic valve, so S2 is heard as two sounds. This physiological splitting is normal.
optWhy: Correct: more right-sided filling prolongs right ventricular ejection, so the pulmonary component comes later.
Inspiration transiently reduces left-sided return (blood pools in the expanding pulmonary vessels), so it does not delay aortic closure.
Mitral and tricuspid closure make the first heart sound, not the second.
A septal defect would be abnormal; this is a normal finding in a healthy young person.
questions.clue: Splitting of S2 on inspiration only, in a healthy young adult.
questions.concept: Timing of valve closure and its relationship to venous return.

followUp.q: In a healthy person, why is the second heart sound heard as a single sound during expiration?
options: The pulmonary valve does not close during expiration
The aortic valve closes silently during expiration
Right and left ventricular ejection end at nearly the same time, so the aortic and pulmonary valves close almost together
Expiration delays aortic closure until after pulmonary closure
followUp.why: Without the extra inspiratory venous return to the right side, right ventricular ejection is not prolonged, so A2 and P2 almost coincide. Both valves close every beat; neither closes silently, and expiration does not reverse their order.

questions.q: Describe the normal sequence of electrical conduction through the heart and explain the importance of the delay at the atrioventricular node.
markScheme: Impulse starts at the SA node in the right atrium (normal pacemaker)
Spreads across both atria causing atrial depolarisation/contraction
Delayed at the AV node, then passes down the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres to the ventricles
AV delay allows the atria to finish emptying into the ventricles before ventricular contraction (and limits the ventricular rate)
questions.modelAnswer: Each beat normally starts at the sinoatrial node in the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava. The impulse spreads across both atria, which depolarise and contract. It then reaches the atrioventricular node, where conduction slows. From there it travels down the bundle of His, the left and right bundle branches and the Purkinje fibres, so the ventricles depolarise rapidly, starting from the septum and apex. The delay at the AV node means the atria complete their contraction and top up ventricular filling before the ventricles contract. It also limits how many impulses reach the ventricles if the atrial rate becomes very fast.
questions.concept: Sequence of cardiac conduction and the role of AV nodal delay.

questions.q: If the radius of an arteriole halves while length and blood viscosity stay the same, how does its resistance to flow change?
options: It falls to one-sixteenth
It rises 16-fold
It doubles
It rises 4-fold
questions.why: By Poiseuille's relationship resistance is proportional to viscosity × length ÷ r⁴, so halving r raises resistance 2⁴ = 16-fold. This steep dependence is why small changes in arteriolar tone control blood flow to organs.
optWhy: This assumes resistance is simply inversely proportional to radius.
This uses r², as if only cross-sectional area mattered.
This uses the right power but the wrong direction: a narrower vessel has more resistance.
Correct: resistance ∝ 1/r⁴, so halving r multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16.
questions.clue: Radius halves; length and viscosity unchanged.
questions.concept: Poiseuille: resistance varies with 1/r⁴.

followUp.q: An arteriole's radius falls by 20% (to 0.8 of its original value) with no other change. Approximately how does its resistance change?
options: It rises 1.25-fold
It rises about 2.4-fold
It rises about 1.6-fold
It falls to about 0.4 of its original value
followUp.why: Resistance ∝ 1/r⁴, so it changes by 1/0.8⁴ = 1/0.41 ≈ 2.44. 1.25-fold uses 1/r; about 1.6-fold uses 1/r² (1/0.64); 0.4 is 0.8⁴, which forgets that resistance rises as radius falls.

questions.q: A patient's blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg at rest. What is the best estimate of mean arterial pressure?
options: About 107 mmHg
100 mmHg
40 mmHg
About 93 mmHg
questions.why: MAP ≈ diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure = 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg, because at rest the heart spends about twice as long in diastole as in systole.
optWhy: This is the simple average of systolic and diastolic, which ignores the longer time spent in diastole.
This is the pulse pressure (120 − 80), not a mean pressure.
Correct: 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.
This subtracts one-third of the pulse pressure from systolic, which weights the mean towards systole.
questions.concept: Estimating MAP from systolic and diastolic pressures.

followUp.q: A patient's resting blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. What is the best estimate of mean arterial pressure?
options: About 110 mmHg
120 mmHg
60 mmHg
About 130 mmHg
followUp.why: MAP ≈ 90 + (150 − 90)/3 = 90 + 20 = 110 mmHg. 120 mmHg is the simple average; 60 mmHg is the pulse pressure; about 130 mmHg subtracts one-third of the pulse pressure from systolic.

questions.q: Echocardiography shows an end-diastolic volume of 130 mL and an end-systolic volume of 60 mL; heart rate is 80/min. Which set of values is correct?
options: Stroke volume 70 mL, cardiac output 10.4 L/min, ejection fraction about 54%
Stroke volume 60 mL, cardiac output 4.8 L/min, ejection fraction about 46%
Stroke volume 70 mL, cardiac output 5.6 L/min, ejection fraction about 46%
Stroke volume 70 mL, cardiac output 5.6 L/min, ejection fraction about 54%
questions.why: Stroke volume = EDV − ESV = 70 mL. Cardiac output = HR × SV = 80 × 70 mL = 5.6 L/min. Ejection fraction = SV ÷ EDV = 70/130 ≈ 54%, at the lower edge of normal (above roughly 50–55%).
optWhy: This treats the end-systolic volume as the stroke volume (60 × 80 = 4.8 L/min; 60/130 ≈ 46%).
Stroke volume and cardiac output are right, but the ejection fraction has been calculated as ESV ÷ EDV (60/130) instead of SV ÷ EDV.
This multiplies end-diastolic volume, not stroke volume, by heart rate (130 × 80 = 10.4 L/min).
questions.concept: CO = HR × SV; SV = EDV − ESV; EF = SV ÷ EDV.

followUp.q: A patient with heart failure has an end-diastolic volume of 160 mL and an ejection fraction of 25%. What is the stroke volume?
options: 40 mL
120 mL
135 mL
640 mL
followUp.why: SV = EF × EDV = 0.25 × 160 = 40 mL. 120 mL is the end-systolic volume (the 75% left behind). 135 mL subtracts 25 from 160 as if EF were a volume. 640 mL divides EDV by 0.25 instead of multiplying.

questions.q: Explain how the baroreceptor reflex maintains blood pressure when a person stands up quickly.
markScheme: Standing causes venous pooling in the legs, reducing venous return, preload and stroke volume, so arterial pressure falls
Reduced stretch of carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors lowers their firing (via CN IX and CN X) to the medulla
Increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic (vagal) outflow
Heart rate and contractility rise (β1); arteriolar constriction raises TPR; venoconstriction increases venous return
Pressure is restored within seconds (MAP ≈ CO × TPR); failure gives postural hypotension
questions.modelAnswer: On standing, gravity pools blood in the veins of the legs. Venous return and preload fall, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall and arterial pressure drops. The baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch are stretched less and fire less, sending fewer impulses along the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the cardiovascular centres in the medulla. The medulla responds by increasing sympathetic outflow and reducing vagal outflow. Heart rate and contractility rise through β1 receptors, arterioles constrict so total peripheral resistance rises, and veins constrict, pushing blood back towards the heart. Because mean arterial pressure is approximately cardiac output × total peripheral resistance, these changes restore pressure within seconds. If the reflex fails, for example in autonomic dysfunction, the person develops postural hypotension and may feel faint.
questions.concept: Baroreceptor reflex control of blood pressure.

questions.q: In early atherosclerosis, which cells take up oxidised LDL in the intima to become foam cells and form the fatty streak?
options: Macrophages derived from monocytes
Neutrophils
Platelets
Endothelial cells
questions.why: Monocytes are attracted to damaged endothelium, enter the intima and become macrophages, which take up oxidised LDL and become foam cells. Collections of foam cells form the fatty streak, an early lesion of atherosclerosis.
optWhy: Neutrophils are the classic cells of acute inflammation, not the lipid-laden cells of the fatty streak.
Platelets matter later, forming thrombus when a plaque ruptures.
Endothelial cells are where injury begins and they let LDL and monocytes in, but they do not become foam cells.
Correct: monocytes enter the intima, become macrophages and engulf oxidised LDL.
questions.concept: Cellular steps in early atherosclerosis.

followUp.q: Which cells migrate into the intima and lay down collagen to form the fibrous cap of a mature plaque?
options: Endothelial cells
Smooth muscle cells
Neutrophils
Platelets
followUp.why: Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima and produce collagen, forming the fibrous cap over the lipid-rich core. Endothelial cells line the lumen; neutrophils and platelets do not build the cap.

questions.q: Why does rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque often cause sudden myocardial infarction even when the plaque was causing little narrowing beforehand?
options: The fibrous cap calcifies instantly and blocks the lumen
The ruptured plaque releases cholesterol crystals that dissolve the myocardium
Exposure of the thrombogenic core triggers platelet aggregation and a thrombus that occludes the artery
Rupture causes immediate coronary spasm, which is the main cause of infarction
questions.why: When the fibrous cap ruptures, the lipid core and collagen are exposed to blood. Platelets adhere and aggregate and the clotting cascade forms a thrombus that can suddenly occlude the artery. Thin-capped, lipid-rich plaques are prone to this even when they caused little narrowing.
optWhy: Cholesterol crystals do not dissolve heart muscle; damage comes from loss of blood supply.
Correct: the exposed lipid core and collagen activate platelets and clotting, and the thrombus can suddenly block the artery.
Vasospasm can contribute, but thrombus is the main mechanism after rupture.
Calcification develops slowly over years; it does not happen instantly at rupture.
questions.clue: 'Little narrowing beforehand' yet a sudden infarct.
questions.concept: Plaque rupture with thrombosis causes acute coronary syndromes.

followUp.q: Which plaque is most likely to rupture and cause an acute coronary syndrome?
options: One with a thick fibrous cap and a small lipid core
A fatty streak in a 20-year-old
One made mainly of smooth muscle and collagen with little lipid
One with a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid core and many inflammatory cells
followUp.why: Vulnerable plaques have thin, inflamed caps over large lipid cores. Thick-capped, collagen-rich plaques are stable and tend to cause exertional symptoms by narrowing. A fatty streak is an early lesion and has no fibrous cap to rupture.

questions.q: A 50-year-old has a clinic blood pressure of 152/94 mmHg on repeated readings. Daytime ambulatory monitoring averages 141/88 mmHg. Using NICE NG136, how is this classified?
options: Not hypertension, because the ambulatory average is below 140/90 mmHg
White-coat effect only, because clinic and ambulatory readings differ
Stage 1 hypertension
Stage 2 hypertension
questions.why: NG136 diagnoses hypertension when clinic BP is 140/90 or more and the ABPM daytime (or HBPM) average is 135/85 or more. Stage 1 is clinic 140/90 to 159/99 with an average of 135/85 to 149/94, which fits these readings. (Guidance as checked October 2026.)
optWhy: Correct: clinic 140/90 to 159/99 with an ambulatory average of 135/85 to 149/94 is stage 1.
Stage 2 needs clinic 160/100 or more with an average of 150/95 or more.
This applies the clinic threshold to the ambulatory average; for ABPM/HBPM the threshold is 135/85.

NICE NG136 defines a white-coat effect as a clinic–ambulatory discrepancy of more than 20/10 mmHg; here it is only 11/6, and in any case the ambulatory average (141/88) is above 135/85, so hypertension is confirmed rather than explained away.
questions.concept: NICE NG136 diagnostic thresholds and stages.

followUp.q: Clinic BP is 166/102 mmHg on repeated readings and the home monitoring average is 152/96 mmHg. Using NICE NG136, how is this classified?
options: Stage 1 hypertension
Severe hypertension
Stage 2 hypertension
Not hypertension
followUp.why: Stage 2 is clinic 160/100 or more (below 180/120) with an ABPM or HBPM average of 150/95 or more, which fits. Stage 1 would need clinic below 160/100 and an average below 150/95. Severe hypertension needs a clinic systolic of 180 or more or diastolic of 120 or more. Both clinic and home averages are above the diagnostic thresholds.

questions.q: Three days after hip replacement surgery, a 68-year-old woman who has barely moved develops a swollen, painful calf. How does Virchow's triad best explain her risk?
options: Stasis from immobility, with hypercoagulability and vessel-wall injury after surgery
Raised arterial pressure, high LDL cholesterol and smoking
Turbulent arterial flow at a branch point damaging the endothelium
Stasis in the left atrium from atrial fibrillation
questions.why: Virchow's triad (venous stasis, hypercoagulability and vessel-wall injury) explains venous thromboembolism. Immobility causes stasis, and major surgery both activates clotting and can injure veins, so all three combine here to produce a deep-vein thrombosis.
optWhy: These are risk factors for arterial atherosclerosis, not for venous thrombosis.
Disturbed arterial flow promotes atherosclerotic plaques, not deep-vein thrombosis.
Left atrial stasis in atrial fibrillation causes clots that embolise to the systemic arteries (e.g. stroke), not calf DVT.
Correct: all three elements of Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, vessel-wall injury) are present after major orthopaedic surgery with immobility.
questions.clue: Recent hip surgery, immobility and a swollen calf.
questions.concept: Virchow's triad explains the risk factors for venous thrombosis.

followUp.q: A 34-year-old taking a combined oral contraceptive develops a deep-vein thrombosis after a long-haul flight. Which elements of Virchow's triad are best illustrated?
options: Vessel-wall injury from atherosclerotic plaque in the leg veins
Hypercoagulability (oestrogen) and stasis (prolonged sitting)
Stasis alone, because the pill has no effect on clotting
Plaque rupture with platelet-rich thrombus
followUp.why: Oestrogen-containing medicines raise clotting-factor activity (hypercoagulability) and a long flight causes venous stasis. Atherosclerosis and plaque rupture are arterial processes, and the pill does affect clotting, which is why it is a recognised VTE risk factor.

questions.q: Outline the stages in the development of an atherosclerotic plaque and explain how risk factors such as smoking and hypertension contribute.
markScheme: Endothelial dysfunction/injury is the initiating step; smoking and hypertension damage the endothelium
LDL enters the intima and is oxidised; monocytes enter and become macrophages
Macrophages take up oxidised LDL to become foam cells, forming the fatty streak
Smooth muscle cells migrate and produce collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a lipid/necrotic core
Complications: thin-capped plaque ruptures, platelets aggregate and thrombus forms (acute coronary syndrome/stroke)
questions.modelAnswer: Atherosclerosis starts with endothelial dysfunction. Smoking (through toxins and oxidative stress) and hypertension (through mechanical stress) damage the endothelium, making it more permeable and more adhesive. LDL cholesterol enters the intima, where it becomes oxidised. Monocytes are attracted, cross the endothelium and become macrophages, which engulf oxidised LDL and become foam cells; collections of foam cells form the fatty streak. Over time smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and produce collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a core of lipid and dead cells. A stable plaque narrows the lumen slowly and may cause angina on exertion. If the cap is thin and inflamed it may rupture, exposing the thrombogenic core; platelets aggregate and a thrombus forms, which can occlude the artery and cause myocardial infarction or stroke.
questions.concept: Stages of atherosclerosis and how risk factors act on them.

questions.q: Which pattern of lung damage is typical of emphysema caused by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
options: Interstitial fibrosis with a restrictive pattern
Panacinar emphysema, worst in the lower lobes
Mucous gland hyperplasia without alveolar wall destruction
Centriacinar emphysema, worst in the upper lobes
questions.why: Lack of alpha-1 antitrypsin leaves neutrophil elastase unchecked throughout the acinus, giving panacinar emphysema, mainly in the lower lobes and often at a younger age. Smoking typically causes centriacinar emphysema in the upper lobes.
optWhy: Centriacinar, upper-lobe emphysema is the pattern usually caused by smoking.
Interstitial fibrosis is a restrictive disease, not emphysema.
Correct: unopposed neutrophil elastase damages the whole acinus, mainly in the lower lobes.
Mucous gland hyperplasia without alveolar destruction describes chronic bronchitis.
questions.concept: Protease–antiprotease balance and emphysema patterns.

followUp.q: A 38-year-old who has never smoked has progressive breathlessness; CT shows emphysema mainly in the lower lobes. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Unopposed neutrophil elastase because of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Mucous gland hyperplasia from chronic bronchitis
Type 2 eosinophilic airway inflammation
Interstitial collagen deposition
followUp.why: Lower-lobe emphysema in a young non-smoker suggests alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: without the antiprotease, elastase destroys alveolar walls. Mucous gland hyperplasia is chronic bronchitis, eosinophilic inflammation is typical of asthma, and collagen deposition is fibrosis, a restrictive disease.

questions.q: A 58-year-old has pre-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV₁ 1.5 L and FVC 3.0 L (FVC is below predicted). How should this pattern be described?
options: Restrictive, because the FVC is reduced
Normal, because FEV₁ is expected to be about half of FVC
Obstructive, because the FEV₁/FVC ratio is 0.5
Obstructive and fully reversible, so it must be asthma
questions.why: FEV₁/FVC = 1.5/3.0 = 0.5, below 0.7, so the pattern is obstructive. FVC can be reduced in obstruction because air trapping limits how much can be exhaled; the ratio, not FVC alone, decides the pattern.
optWhy: Restriction gives a normal or high ratio; FVC can also be low in obstruction because air is trapped.
A normal FEV₁/FVC ratio is usually above 0.7, not about 0.5.
Correct: 1.5/3.0 = 0.5, below the 0.7 threshold.
Reversibility cannot be judged from a single pre-bronchodilator test, so it cannot show the obstruction is reversible or prove asthma.
questions.concept: Interpreting spirometry using FEV₁/FVC.

followUp.q: A 60-year-old with pulmonary fibrosis has FEV₁ 2.0 L and FVC 2.3 L, both below predicted. How should this pattern be described?
options: Restrictive: FVC is reduced with a normal or high ratio (about 0.87)
Obstructive, because FEV₁ is reduced
Normal, because the ratio is above 0.7
Mixed obstructive and restrictive, because both values are reduced
followUp.why: The ratio is 2.0/2.3 ≈ 0.87 (normal or high) and FVC is reduced, which is restrictive, as expected in fibrosis. A low FEV₁ alone does not mean obstruction when FVC is low too. A normal ratio does not make the test normal if FVC is reduced, and a mixed pattern would need a low ratio as well.

questions.q: A 72-year-old with community-acquired pneumonia is newly confused. Urea is 9 mmol/L, respiratory rate 32/min and blood pressure 104/64 mmHg. What is the CURB-65 score?
questions.why: Confusion (1), urea above 7 mmol/L (1), respiratory rate 30/min or more (1), blood pressure systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 or less (0 here), age 65 or over (1): total 4. Higher scores indicate more severe pneumonia.
optWhy: This wrongly scores blood pressure: 104/64 is neither systolic below 90 nor diastolic 60 or less.
This misses one point, most often the age criterion (65 or over).
This counts only two criteria, missing two of urea, respiratory rate or age.
Correct: confusion 1, urea above 7 mmol/L 1, respiratory rate 30 or more 1, age 65 or over 1; blood pressure scores 0.
questions.clue: New confusion, urea 9, RR 32, BP 104/64, age 72.
questions.concept: Applying CURB-65 criteria exactly.

followUp.q: A 58-year-old with pneumonia is alert. Urea is 8.2 mmol/L, respiratory rate 24/min and blood pressure 88/58 mmHg. What is the CURB-65 score?
followUp.why: Urea above 7 (1) and low blood pressure (1, as systolic is below 90; the diastolic of 58 also qualifies but the BP criterion scores only once). Not confused, rate below 30 and under 65, so the total is 2. Scoring BP twice gives 3.

questions.q: Compare asthma and COPD in terms of cause, typical patient, mechanism of airflow obstruction and reversibility.
markScheme: Asthma: often atopic, frequently starts in childhood/young adulthood; COPD: usually older adult with significant smoking history (or other exposures)
Asthma: chronic (often eosinophilic/Th2) airway inflammation with hyper-responsiveness and bronchoconstriction
COPD: chronic bronchitis (mucus hypersecretion) and emphysema (alveolar wall destruction, loss of elastic recoil, airway collapse)
Asthma: obstruction variable and largely reversible; symptoms vary, e.g. worse at night
COPD: persistent, progressive obstruction not fully reversible; FEV₁/FVC < 0.7 post-bronchodilator
questions.modelAnswer: Asthma often begins in childhood or young adulthood and is linked to atopy and family history, with triggers such as allergens, viral infections, exercise and cold air. COPD usually affects older adults with a significant smoking history, though occupational dusts and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency also cause it. In asthma, chronic airway inflammation (often type 2, with eosinophils, mast cells and IgE) makes the airways hyper-responsive, so smooth muscle constricts, the wall swells and mucus is produced. In COPD, chronic bronchitis narrows the airways with mucus and inflammation, and emphysema destroys alveolar walls; the loss of elastic recoil lets small airways collapse during expiration and traps air. Asthma's obstruction is variable and largely reversible, so symptoms and peak flow fluctuate. COPD's obstruction is persistent and progressive and is not fully reversible, defined in NICE guidance by a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7.
questions.concept: Distinguishing asthma from COPD by mechanism and reversibility.

questions.q: On what principle does a pulse oximeter estimate arterial oxygen saturation?
options: Different absorption of red and infrared light by oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin in the pulsatile signal
Electrochemical detection of oxygen in capillary blood
Detection of carbon dioxide in the arterial pulse wave
Measurement of the partial pressure of dissolved oxygen through the skin
questions.why: Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb red and infrared light differently. By analysing only the pulsatile part of the signal the device estimates arterial saturation. Because it is optical, poor perfusion, movement, nail varnish and carboxyhaemoglobin can all mislead it.
optWhy: Oximetry estimates saturation, not partial pressure; PaO₂ needs a blood gas.
Correct: the ratio of red to infrared absorption in the pulsatile (arterial) component gives SpO₂.
No electrode or blood sample is involved; it is an optical method.
Pulse oximetry gives no information about CO₂.
questions.concept: How pulse oximetry works and its limitations.

followUp.q: A man rescued from a house fire is confused and has a headache. A standard pulse oximeter reads 99%. What is the best explanation?
options: His oxygen delivery must be normal because SpO₂ is 99%
Smoke particles make the probe read low, so true saturation is even higher
Carbon monoxide shifts the curve right, so tissues receive extra oxygen
Carboxyhaemoglobin is read as oxyhaemoglobin, so the SpO₂ is falsely reassuring
followUp.why: Standard oximeters cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ looks normal although oxygen content is reduced; co-oximetry on a blood gas is needed. Carbon monoxide shifts the curve left, not right, further reducing unloading.

questions.q: An ECG recorded at the standard 25 mm/s shows a regular rhythm with four large squares between consecutive R waves. What is the heart rate?
options: 375 beats/min
15 beats/min
150 beats/min
75 beats/min
questions.why: Each large square is 0.2 s at 25 mm/s, so the R–R interval is 0.8 s and the rate is 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min. Equivalently, 300 ÷ 4 large squares or 1,500 ÷ 20 small squares.
optWhy: This applies the small-square rule (1,500 ÷ squares) to large squares.
This divides 300 by the number of small squares (20), mixing up the two rules.
This would be the result at a paper speed of 50 mm/s, when each large square is 0.1 s.
questions.clue: Regular rhythm; four large squares between R waves at 25 mm/s.
questions.concept: ECG rate calculation from the R–R interval.

followUp.q: A 10-second rhythm strip shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with 18 QRS complexes. What is the estimated ventricular rate?
options: 180 beats/min
18 beats/min
108 beats/min
75 beats/min
followUp.why: For irregular rhythms count complexes in 10 seconds and multiply by 6: 18 × 6 = 108. Multiplying by 10 gives 180; 18 is the raw count; 75 would come from applying the 300 ÷ large-squares rule to one R–R interval, which is unreliable when intervals vary.

questions.q: A patient with COPD who is known to be at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure is acutely unwell. Under British Thoracic Society guidance, what oxygen saturation should be targeted?
options: Below 85%, to avoid suppressing the hypoxic drive
questions.why: The BTS guideline (2017, still current as checked in October 2026) sets 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, because too much oxygen can worsen CO₂ retention, and 94–98% for most other acutely ill adults. Hypoxaemia must still be corrected.
optWhy: 94–98% is the target for most other acutely ill adults, so this misapplies the general target.
Aiming for 98–100% reflects the mistaken belief that more oxygen is always safer; it can worsen CO₂ retention here.
Deliberately keeping saturation below 85% overstates the hypoxic-drive concern and would leave the patient dangerously hypoxaemic.
Correct: BTS sets 88–92% for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
questions.clue: COPD 'at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure'.
questions.concept: Choosing the BTS target saturation range for a patient group.

followUp.q: A 45-year-old with pneumonia and no chronic lung disease is acutely unwell with SpO₂ 89% on air. Under BTS guidance, which target range applies?
followUp.why: Without risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure, BTS sets 94–98% for acutely ill adults. 88–92% is only for people at risk of hypercapnia; 100% is not a target; 85–88% would leave her hypoxaemic.

questions.q: Describe how to measure blood pressure manually with a sphygmomanometer and stethoscope, and give three sources of error.
markScheme: Patient seated, rested, arm supported at heart level; correct cuff size over the brachial artery
Inflate cuff above systolic (e.g. estimate by palpating radial pulse disappearance), then deflate slowly
Systolic = first Korotkoff sound (phase I); diastolic = disappearance of sounds (phase V)
Errors: wrong cuff size (small cuff overestimates), arm not at heart level, talking/recent exercise/caffeine/smoking, white-coat effect, deflating too fast
Repeat the measurement and record arm and position
questions.modelAnswer: The patient should sit and rest for a few minutes, with the arm bared and supported at heart level. Choose a cuff whose bladder fits the arm, and place it on the upper arm over the brachial artery. Estimate systolic pressure by inflating the cuff until the radial pulse disappears, then deflate. Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery, inflate to about 20–30 mmHg above that estimate, and deflate slowly. The first Korotkoff sound (phase I) is the systolic pressure and the point where the sounds disappear (phase V) is the diastolic. Record the reading, the arm used and the position, and repeat if it is raised. Sources of error include a cuff that is too small (overestimates) or too large (underestimates), the arm hanging below heart level, the patient talking or having recently exercised, smoked or drunk caffeine, deflating too quickly, and the white-coat effect.
questions.concept: Accurate manual blood pressure measurement and its errors.

questions.q: Why do ACE inhibitors commonly cause a dry cough?
options: Angiotensin II builds up in the lungs
They block β2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle
Bradykinin accumulates because ACE normally breaks it down
Aldosterone levels rise and cause airway oedema
questions.why: Angiotensin-converting enzyme also breaks down bradykinin. ACE inhibitors therefore raise bradykinin, which causes the typical dry cough and, rarely, angioedema. ARBs block the AT1 receptor without affecting bradykinin, so cough is uncommon with them.
optWhy: Angiotensin II falls rather than builds up, because its production is blocked.
β2 blockade is a property of non-selective beta-blockers, which can cause bronchospasm, not of ACE inhibitors.
Correct: ACE also degrades bradykinin, so inhibiting it lets bradykinin accumulate and irritate the airways.
Aldosterone falls, not rises, with ACE inhibition.
questions.concept: Adverse effects follow from a drug's mechanism.

followUp.q: A patient taking an ACE inhibitor has a persistent dry cough. Which class would keep blockade of the renin–angiotensin system while avoiding the mechanism of the cough?
options: An angiotensin II receptor blocker
A non-selective beta-blocker
A different ACE inhibitor
A loop diuretic
followUp.why: An ARB blocks the AT1 receptor, so angiotensin II's effects are still blocked, but ACE is not inhibited and bradykinin does not accumulate. Another ACE inhibitor would cause the same cough; beta-blockers and loop diuretics act on different systems.

questions.q: How does salbutamol relieve bronchoconstriction?
options: It blocks muscarinic M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle
It suppresses inflammatory gene transcription in airway cells
It stimulates β2 receptors, raising cAMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
It blocks cysteinyl leukotriene receptors
questions.why: Salbutamol stimulates β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle; the rise in cAMP causes relaxation and bronchodilation. Its effects on β2 receptors elsewhere explain tremor, tachycardia and low potassium.
optWhy: Blocking M3 receptors is how muscarinic antagonists such as ipratropium and tiotropium work.
Suppressing inflammatory gene transcription describes inhaled corticosteroids.
Correct: salbutamol is a short-acting β2 agonist.
Blocking leukotriene receptors describes montelukast.
questions.concept: Mechanisms of bronchodilators.

followUp.q: A patient using a short-acting β2 agonist very frequently develops a fine tremor and a low serum potassium. What is the best explanation?
options: β2 stimulation drives potassium into cells and causes skeletal-muscle tremor
Muscarinic blockade reduces potassium absorption from the gut
A corticosteroid effect increases potassium loss in urine
β1 blockade slows the heart and lowers potassium
followUp.why: β2 agonists stimulate the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, shifting K⁺ into cells, and act on skeletal-muscle β2 receptors to cause tremor. Salbutamol is not a muscarinic antagonist, a corticosteroid or a β1 blocker.

questions.q: A 62-year-old man of white British family origin who does not have diabetes has confirmed stage 2 hypertension. Under NICE NG136, which class is usually offered at step 1, alongside lifestyle advice?
options: A thiazide-like diuretic
A beta-blocker
A calcium-channel blocker
An ACE inhibitor or ARB
questions.why: NG136 bases step 1 on age, family origin and type 2 diabetes. Aged 55 or over without type 2 diabetes, he would usually be offered a calcium-channel blocker, with lifestyle advice throughout. (Guidance as checked October 2026; no doses given.)
optWhy: An ACE inhibitor or ARB is step 1 for people with type 2 diabetes, or under 55 and not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin.
NG136 does not use a thiazide-like diuretic as the usual step 1 choice for this man.
Beta-blockers are not a routine step 1 treatment for hypertension in NG136.
Correct: people aged 55 or over without type 2 diabetes start with a calcium-channel blocker.
questions.concept: NICE NG136 step 1 choice by age, family origin and diabetes.

followUp.q: A 48-year-old woman of Black African family origin with type 2 diabetes needs step 1 antihypertensive treatment. Under NICE NG136, which is preferred?
options: A calcium-channel blocker, because of her family origin
An ARB, in preference to an ACE inhibitor
An ACE inhibitor combined with an ARB
A beta-blocker
followUp.why: People with type 2 diabetes start with an ACE inhibitor or ARB whatever their age or family origin, and for people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin NICE advises considering an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor. The calcium-channel blocker route applies to those without type 2 diabetes. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined.

questions.q: A 30-year-old has just been diagnosed with asthma after objective testing. Under the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN guideline, which treatment approach is recommended first?
options: An as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol inhaler (AIR therapy)
A leukotriene receptor antagonist alone
A long-acting muscarinic antagonist alone
A short-acting β2 agonist alone, used as needed
questions.why: NG245/SIGN 244 recommends as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (anti-inflammatory reliever, AIR) for newly diagnosed people aged 12 and over (people who are highly symptomatic at diagnosis start on MART instead), stepping up to maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) if not controlled. Every step includes an inhaled corticosteroid. (Guidance as checked October 2026; no doses given.)
optWhy: The 2024 guideline advises against prescribing a SABA without an inhaled corticosteroid.
Correct: newly diagnosed people aged 12 and over start with as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol.
Leukotriene receptor antagonists are considered later, as add-on trials, not as first treatment.
LAMAs are considered as add-on trials later, not first-line alone.
questions.clue: Newly diagnosed asthma in an adult.
questions.concept: Current UK principle: asthma treatment always includes an inhaled corticosteroid.

followUp.q: Why does the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma guideline advise against prescribing a short-acting β2 agonist without an inhaled corticosteroid?
options: SABAs block M3 receptors and thicken airway mucus
SABAs cause bronchospasm by blocking β2 receptors
SABAs take several weeks to start working
A SABA relieves bronchospasm but does not treat the underlying airway inflammation
followUp.why: SABAs relax smooth muscle quickly but leave the airway inflammation untreated; inhaled corticosteroids treat the inflammation. SABAs stimulate (not block) β2 receptors, do not act on M3 receptors and work within minutes.

questions.q: Explain how aspirin and statins each reduce the risk of further events in a patient who has had a myocardial infarction.
markScheme: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1)
Reduces thromboxane A₂, so less platelet aggregation and thrombus formation on plaques, for the platelet's lifetime
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis; liver up-regulates LDL receptors so plasma LDL falls
Lower LDL slows plaque growth and stabilises plaques, so fewer ruptures
questions.modelAnswer: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-1 in platelets. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so thromboxane A₂ production is reduced for the rest of the platelet's life. Less thromboxane means less platelet activation and aggregation, so a thrombus is less likely to form on a damaged plaque. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. Liver cells respond by making more LDL receptors, which remove LDL from the blood. Lower LDL slows plaque growth, and statins are thought to help stabilise plaques, so fewer rupture and cause further heart attacks or strokes.
questions.concept: Mechanisms of antiplatelet and lipid-lowering drugs in secondary prevention.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the parameters scored in NEWS2?
options: Capillary refill time
Respiration rate
Whether the patient is receiving supplemental oxygen
Level of consciousness or new confusion
questions.why: NEWS2 scores respiration rate, oxygen saturation, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, level of consciousness or new confusion, and temperature, and adds points for supplemental oxygen. Capillary refill is assessed in ABCDE but not scored.
optWhy: Correct: capillary refill time is part of an ABCDE assessment but is not scored in NEWS2.
Respiration rate is scored, and is often the earliest sign of deterioration.
Being on supplemental oxygen adds points, which students sometimes overlook because it is not a vital sign.
Level of consciousness, including new confusion, is scored.
questions.concept: Components of NEWS2.

followUp.q: A ward patient's observations are unchanged, but they have just been started on supplemental oxygen. How does this affect their NEWS2 total?
options: It has no effect, because only vital signs are scored
It lowers the total, because the saturation will now be normal
It increases the total, because supplemental oxygen is scored
It counts only if saturation falls below 88%
followUp.why: NEWS2 adds points when a patient needs supplemental oxygen, because needing oxygen is itself a sign of illness. It is not limited to vital signs and does not depend on a particular saturation threshold.

questions.q: A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 80%. It is used in a population where 10% have the disease. What is its positive predictive value?
options: About 33%
About 98.6%
questions.why: In 1,000 people, 100 have the disease (90 true positives, 10 false negatives) and 900 do not (720 true negatives, 180 false positives). PPV = 90/(90 + 180) ≈ 33%. At low prevalence even a fairly good test produces many false positives.
optWhy: 90% is the sensitivity, a common confusion with PPV.
80% is the specificity.
About 98.6% is the negative predictive value (720 true negatives out of 730 negative results).
Correct: in 1,000 people, 90 true positives and 180 false positives, so 90/270 ≈ 33%.
questions.concept: Predictive values depend on prevalence; build a 2 × 2 table.

followUp.q: The same test (sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%) is used in a clinic where 50% of those tested have the disease. What is the PPV now?
options: About 33%
About 82%
About 89%
followUp.why: In 1,000 people: 500 diseased (450 true positives) and 500 not (100 false positives), so PPV = 450/550 ≈ 82%. About 33% was the PPV at 10% prevalence; 90% is the sensitivity; about 89% is the NPV here (400 true negatives out of 450 negatives). Higher prevalence raises PPV.

questions.q: A ward patient has noisy inspiratory stridor, SpO₂ 88% on air, heart rate 120/min and blood pressure 92/58 mmHg. Following the ABCDE approach, what should be dealt with first?
options: The low blood pressure
The low saturation, by obtaining a blood gas before any other step
The airway obstruction
Taking a full history to establish the diagnosis
questions.why: ABCDE (Resuscitation Council UK) deals with problems in order of threat to life and treats each problem as it is found before moving on, calling for help early and reassessing after each intervention. Stridor indicates upper airway obstruction, so the airway comes first.
optWhy: Circulation matters, but it comes after airway and breathing problems have been addressed.
Oxygenation is part of breathing, but an obstructed airway must be dealt with first, and investigations should not delay treatment.
Correct: stridor signals airway obstruction, which is the most immediate threat to life and is treated first.
A full history comes after immediate threats to life have been treated.
questions.clue: Stridor (an airway sign) alongside abnormal breathing and circulation.
questions.concept: ABCDE assesses and treats in order of threat to life.

followUp.q: Following the ABCDE approach, you give a treatment for a breathing problem. What should you do next?
options: Reassess the patient to check the effect of the treatment
Move straight on to Disability without reassessing
Wait until the whole assessment is complete before treating anything else
Hand over to another team without reassessing
followUp.why: Resuscitation Council UK advises checking the effects of treatment and reassessing regularly. Moving on without reassessing or delaying treatment until the end goes against the approach, which treats problems as they are found.

questions.q: Define sensitivity and specificity, and explain why a negative result on a highly sensitive test is useful for ruling out a disease.
markScheme: Sensitivity: proportion of people with the disease who test positive (TP ÷ (TP + FN))
Specificity: proportion of people without the disease who test negative (TN ÷ (TN + FP))
A highly sensitive test produces few false negatives
So a negative result makes the disease unlikely ('SnNOut'), especially when pre-test probability is not high
questions.modelAnswer: Sensitivity is the proportion of people who have the disease who test positive: true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative: true negatives divided by true negatives plus false positives. A highly sensitive test rarely misses the disease, so it gives few false negatives. If such a test is negative, the disease is therefore unlikely, which is summarised by the phrase 'SnNOut' (sensitive test, negative result, rules out). How confident you can be still depends on the pre-test probability: in a patient with a very high clinical suspicion a negative result may not be enough.
questions.concept: Sensitivity, specificity and ruling a diagnosis out.

questions.q: A healthy 20-year-old student starts a period of moderate running. Explain how the cardiovascular and respiratory systems respond so that delivery of oxygen to working muscle increases and carbon dioxide is removed. Refer to relevant equations and control mechanisms.
markScheme: Cardiac output rises (CO = HR × SV): sympathetic β1 stimulation and reduced vagal tone raise heart rate and contractility
Stroke volume rises: increased venous return (muscle pump, respiratory pump, venoconstriction) increases preload (Frank–Starling) plus increased contractility

Local metabolic vasodilation in muscle (CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine, low O₂) lowers TPR; sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood from gut/skin; systolic BP rises, diastolic changes little (MAP ≈ CO × TPR)

Ventilation rises via increased tidal volume and rate; mechanisms include feed-forward central command and muscle afferents with chemoreceptor fine-tuning (arterial PCO₂ normally kept near normal in moderate exercise)
Rightward shift of O₂–Hb curve in muscle (raised PCO₂, H⁺, temperature) increases unloading; increased capillary recruitment shortens diffusion distance (Fick)
CO₂ carried as bicarbonate/carbamino; Haldane effect; increased pulmonary blood flow and ventilation remove CO₂
Pulmonary capillary recruitment improves V/Q matching and diffusion capacity
Clear structure and correct use of equations and values labelled approximate
questions.modelAnswer:
Working muscle needs much more oxygen, and both systems respond together.

Cardiac output. CO = HR × SV. At the start of exercise, signals from the motor cortex (central command) and from muscle receptors reduce vagal tone and increase sympathetic outflow. Noradrenaline acting on β1 receptors steepens the pacemaker slope of the SA node and raises heart rate, and it increases contractility. Stroke volume also rises because venous return increases: contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins (the muscle pump), deeper breathing lowers intrathoracic pressure (the respiratory pump), and sympathetic venoconstriction mobilises blood from the veins. Greater end-diastolic filling increases the force of contraction by the Frank–Starling mechanism. Cardiac output can rise several-fold, roughly four to five times resting in a fit young adult (approximate).

Distribution of flow and blood pressure. In muscle, local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine and low O₂) dilate arterioles, overriding sympathetic constriction, so muscle blood flow rises greatly and total peripheral resistance falls. Sympathetic vasoconstriction reduces flow to the gut and kidneys, and skin flow later rises for heat loss. Because MAP ≈ CO × TPR, the large rise in CO and fall in TPR mean systolic pressure rises while diastolic pressure changes little.

Ventilation. Minute ventilation rises through deeper and faster breaths. The quick rise at the start is driven by central command and muscle afferents; chemoreceptors (central, responding to CSF H⁺, and peripheral, in the carotid and aortic bodies) fine-tune ventilation so that arterial PCO₂ and PO₂ stay close to normal in moderate exercise. Pulmonary blood flow rises with cardiac output and previously underused capillaries, especially at the lung apices, are recruited, improving V/Q matching and increasing the surface area available for diffusion (Fick's law).

Oxygen unloading. In muscle, raised PCO₂, raised H⁺ and higher temperature shift the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right (the Bohr effect), so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given PO₂. More capillaries open, shortening the diffusion distance. Oxygen extraction therefore increases as well as delivery.

Carbon dioxide removal. Extra CO₂ enters red cells, where carbonic anhydrase converts it to bicarbonate, which leaves in exchange for chloride; some binds haemoglobin as carbamino compounds. Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂ (the Haldane effect). In the lungs, increased ventilation keeps alveolar PCO₂ low, so CO₂ diffuses out and is exhaled.

Together these changes match oxygen delivery and CO₂ removal to the rise in metabolic rate.
questions.concept: Integrated cardiorespiratory response to exercise (CO = HR × SV; MAP ≈ CO × TPR; Bohr and Haldane effects).

questions.q:
A 64-year-old man who has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years has increasing breathlessness on exertion and a morning cough with sputum. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows FEV₁ 1.8 L (60% of predicted), FVC 3.3 L and FEV₁/FVC 0.55.
(a) Calculate his smoking history in pack-years. (2 marks)
(b) Interpret the spirometry and state the most likely diagnosis. (4 marks)
(c) Explain the pathophysiology that causes airflow limitation in this condition. (6 marks)
(d) Explain how an inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist and a long-acting β2 agonist each improve airflow. (4 marks)
(e) Explain why smoking cessation is the most important intervention. (4 marks)
markScheme: (a) 20/20 × 40 = 40 pack-years
(b) FEV₁/FVC 0.55 < 0.7 post-bronchodilator = obstructive pattern not fully reversible; with smoking history and symptoms, most likely COPD
(c) Chronic bronchitis: mucous gland hyperplasia, goblet cells, inflammation and mucus narrow airways

(c) Emphysema (centriacinar in smokers): protease–antiprotease imbalance destroys alveolar walls; loss of elastic recoil and of radial traction lets small airways collapse on expiration; air trapping and hyperinflation
(d) LAMA blocks M3 receptors, preventing vagally mediated (acetylcholine) bronchoconstriction; LABA stimulates β2, raising cAMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
(e) Smoking cessation is the intervention most clearly shown to slow the accelerated decline in FEV₁ in smokers (Fletcher and Peto); also cuts cardiovascular and lung cancer risk
Correct, clearly set out working; no drug doses
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked = (20 ÷ 20) × 40 = 40 pack-years.

(b) The post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio is 0.55, below the 0.7 threshold, so there is airflow obstruction that persists after a bronchodilator and is therefore not fully reversible. FEV₁ is reduced to 60% of predicted. With a 40 pack-year history, exertional breathlessness and a chronic productive cough, the most likely diagnosis is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). By the GOLD spirometric grading, an FEV₁ of 50–79% of predicted is moderate (GOLD 2).

(c) COPD combines chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Cigarette smoke causes chronic inflammation of the airways with neutrophils, macrophages and CD8 T cells. In the larger airways, mucous glands enlarge and goblet cells increase, producing excess mucus that narrows the lumen and causes the productive cough; the airway walls thicken and fibrose. In the lung tissue, proteases such as neutrophil elastase, together with oxidants, overwhelm the antiproteases and destroy alveolar walls. In smokers this is usually centriacinar emphysema, worst in the upper lobes. Destroying alveolar walls removes elastic recoil, which normally drives expiration, and removes the radial traction that holds small airways open. During forced expiration the small airways therefore collapse early, trapping air behind them. This lowers FEV₁ much more than FVC, causes hyperinflation and increases the work of breathing. Loss of alveolar surface area also reduces gas exchange.

(d) A long-acting muscarinic antagonist (such as tiotropium) blocks M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle. Vagal release of acetylcholine is an important cause of airway tone in COPD, so blocking it relaxes the airways and widens them. A long-acting β2 agonist (such as salmeterol or formoterol) stimulates β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle; this raises cAMP and causes relaxation and bronchodilation. Both reduce air trapping and breathlessness, but neither reverses the structural damage.

(e) Smoking is the main cause of his disease. In susceptible smokers FEV₁ falls faster than the normal age-related decline. Stopping smoking is the intervention shown to slow this decline, a finding associated with Fletcher and Peto's work in the 1970s; lung function does not return to normal, but its rate of fall moves back towards that of a non-smoker. Stopping also reduces cough and sputum, the risk of exacerbations, and his high risk of cardiovascular disease and lung cancer. No inhaler slows the decline in the way stopping smoking does, so support to stop (behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy) should be offered at every opportunity.
questions.concept: COPD: spirometric diagnosis, pathophysiology, bronchodilator mechanisms and smoking cessation.

cases.title: Breathless on exertion

steps.text: A 67-year-old retired builder sees his GP with 18 months of gradually worsening breathlessness when walking uphill, and a cough on most mornings bringing up white sputum. He has no chest pain and no weight loss.

ask.q: Which further piece of history would most help narrow the differential at this stage?
options: Whether he had eczema as a child
Whether he has recently taken a long-haul flight
His smoking history in pack-years and any occupational dust exposure
His weekly alcohol intake
ask.why: Slowly progressive exertional breathlessness with a chronic productive cough in an older adult makes COPD a leading possibility, and smoking (in pack-years) and dust exposure are its main causes. Childhood eczema points towards asthma but discriminates less here; a recent flight matters for acute breathlessness from pulmonary embolism rather than an 18-month history; alcohol intake is part of any history but does not narrow this differential much.

steps.text: He smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 36 years, stopping 2 years ago, and worked with cement dust. On examination: respiratory rate 20/min, SpO₂ 93% on air, hyperexpanded chest with reduced expansion, prolonged expiration and scattered wheeze. No ankle oedema; JVP not raised.

options: 45 pack-years
900 pack-years
36 pack-years
About 29 pack-years
ask.why: Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years = (25 ÷ 20) × 36 = 45. 900 multiplies cigarettes by years without dividing by 20; 36 counts years only; about 29 inverts the ratio (20 ÷ 25 × 36).

steps.text: Post-bronchodilator spirometry: FEV₁ 1.6 L (55% of predicted) and FVC 2.9 L. Full blood count is normal and a chest X-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with no mass.

ask.q: How should the spirometry be interpreted?
options: A restrictive pattern, because FVC is reduced
Normal, because FEV₁ is above 1.5 L
Asthma, because FEV₁ is reduced
Persistent obstruction: post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC about 0.55, below 0.7, consistent with COPD
ask.why: FEV₁/FVC = 1.6/2.9 ≈ 0.55. A ratio below 0.7 after a bronchodilator shows obstruction that is not fully reversible, which with this history fits COPD. FVC can fall in obstruction because of air trapping, so a low FVC does not mean restriction when the ratio is low. Absolute FEV₁ must be compared with predicted (here 55%). A reduced FEV₁ alone does not identify asthma, which is characterised by variable, reversible obstruction.

steps.text: Outcome: a diagnosis of COPD is made. The physiology explains his findings: emphysema removes elastic recoil and radial traction, so small airways collapse on expiration, trapping air (hyperexpansion, prolonged expiration). Staying smoke-free is the single most important step for slowing his loss of lung function; inhaled bronchodilators relieve symptoms (details are taught later and no doses are given here). If he becomes acutely unwell and is at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, BTS guidance targets saturations of 88–92%.

debrief: A chronic history of exertional breathlessness with productive cough in a smoker points to COPD; quantify exposure in pack-years.
Interpret spirometry with the ratio first: post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 shows persistent obstruction.
Hyperexpansion and prolonged expiration follow from loss of elastic recoil and air trapping.
Oxygen targets depend on the risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (BTS: 88–92% for those at risk, 94–98% for most others).

cases.title: Chest pain on exertion

steps.text: A 59-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, who smokes, describes a tight, band-like central chest discomfort that comes on when she walks uphill in the cold and settles within 5 minutes of rest. It sometimes spreads to her left arm.

ask.q: Which feature most strongly suggests myocardial ischaemia from a stable plaque?
options: Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Discomfort brought on by exertion and relieved by rest within minutes
Sharp pain that is worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward
Burning pain after large meals that eases with antacids
ask.why: A fixed, stable plaque limits flow so that supply fails only when demand rises: pain on exertion that settles with rest is the pattern of stable angina. Chest-wall tenderness suggests a musculoskeletal cause, positional sharp pain suggests pericarditis, and meal-related burning suggests reflux.

steps.text: Examination is normal apart from a blood pressure of 152/94 mmHg. Her resting 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm at 75/min with normal intervals.

ask.q: What does the normal resting ECG tell you?
options: It excludes coronary artery disease
It does not exclude angina, because ischaemia from a stable plaque often shows only when demand rises
It confirms that the pain is musculoskeletal
It shows she has had a silent myocardial infarction
ask.why: At rest, supply through a stable narrowing can meet demand, so the ECG is often normal between episodes. A normal resting ECG therefore cannot exclude coronary disease or prove another cause, and it shows no sign of a previous infarction.

steps.text: Three weeks later she develops crushing central chest pain at rest lasting 30 minutes, with sweating and nausea.

ask.q: What is the most likely mechanism of this new episode?
options: Gradual growth of her stable plaque over the three weeks
Oesophageal spasm
Pulmonary embolism from a deep-vein thrombosis
Rupture of a thin-capped plaque with platelet-rich thrombus (an acute coronary syndrome)
ask.why: Prolonged pain at rest with sweating and nausea in someone with several cardiovascular risk factors suggests an acute coronary syndrome, usually caused by plaque rupture and thrombosis. Plaques grow slowly over years, not weeks. Oesophageal spasm and pulmonary embolism belong in the differential but fit this picture less well; dangerous causes must still be considered.

steps.text: Pain at rest that does not settle is treated as a possible acute coronary syndrome needing emergency assessment (in the community, call 999). In hospital the team would use an ABCDE approach, record a 12-lead ECG and take blood tests. Her risk factors all promote endothelial damage and plaque formation.

ask.q: Which of her cardiovascular risk factors is non-modifiable?
options: Her age
Smoking
Hypertension
Type 2 diabetes
ask.why: Age cannot be changed. Smoking can be stopped, and blood pressure and diabetes can be controlled, which lowers future risk.

steps.text: Outcome and key learning: stable angina reflects a fixed narrowing that limits supply on exertion; an acute coronary syndrome usually reflects sudden plaque rupture with thrombus. A normal resting ECG does not rule out coronary disease. Reducing modifiable risk factors slows plaque growth and lowers the chance of rupture.

debrief: Exertional pain relieved by rest suggests stable angina; prolonged rest pain suggests an acute coronary syndrome.
Plaque rupture with thrombus, not slow narrowing, causes most acute coronary syndromes.
A normal resting ECG does not exclude coronary disease.
Always consider dangerous differentials (acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection) in chest pain.

osce.title: Cardiovascular examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's name and date of birth, explain the examination, gain consent and ask about any pain
Position the patient at about 45° with the chest appropriately exposed; offer a chaperone and respect dignity
General inspection from the end of the bed: breathlessness, colour, scars, and clues nearby (oxygen, medicines, GTN spray)
Hands: temperature, colour, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, capillary refill time
Radial pulse: rate and rhythm; compare both radial pulses; check for a collapsing pulse after confirming the shoulder is not painful
Blood pressure (measure it, or state that you would)
Face: conjunctival pallor, xanthelasma, corneal arcus, central cyanosis, dental hygiene
Neck: jugular venous pressure with the patient at 45°, then carotid pulse character, one side at a time
Chest inspection: scars (e.g. midline sternotomy), visible pulsation, chest-wall deformity
Palpation: locate the apex beat (normally around the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line) and feel for heaves and thrills

Auscultation: mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary and aortic areas, timing with the carotid pulse; add manoeuvres (left lateral position for mitral, sitting forward in held expiration for aortic) and listen over the carotids
Lung bases for crackles, then the sacrum and ankles for pitting oedema
Thank the patient, help them redress, clean your hands, then summarise findings and suggest further tests (e.g. full observations, 12-lead ECG, peripheral vascular examination)
tips: Time heart sounds against the carotid pulse so you can tell systole from diastole.
Feel the carotid pulse gently, one side at a time, with the patient lying back: pressure on the carotid can cause reflex bradycardia.
Follow your own medical school's mark scheme where its order differs.
Present findings in a structured way: positives first, then relevant negatives, then a likely explanation.

osce.title: Respiratory examination
steps: Clean your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the examination, gain consent and ask about pain
Position the patient at about 45° with the chest appropriately exposed; offer a chaperone
General inspection: breathlessness at rest, use of accessory muscles, pursed-lip breathing, cough, and clues nearby (inhalers, oxygen, sputum pot)
Hands: clubbing, peripheral cyanosis, tar staining, wasting, and a flapping tremor (a sign of CO₂ retention)
Pulse and respiratory rate, counting breaths discreetly for a full minute
Face and neck: central cyanosis (tongue), conjunctival pallor, jugular venous pressure
Trachea position (warn the patient first, as it is uncomfortable) and cricosternal distance
Chest inspection: shape (e.g. hyperexpansion), symmetry, scars
Palpation: chest expansion on both sides and the apex beat
Percussion: compare both sides in each zone, including the axillae; tactile vocal fremitus
Auscultation: compare both sides for breath sounds and added sounds (wheeze, crackles), then vocal resonance
Cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes
Repeat expansion, percussion and auscultation on the posterior chest
Ankles for oedema and calves for signs of deep-vein thrombosis
Thank the patient, clean your hands, summarise findings and suggest further tests (e.g. SpO₂, peak flow, spirometry, chest X-ray)
tips: Always compare like with like on the two sides of the chest.
Dullness to percussion suggests fluid or consolidation; hyper-resonance suggests pneumothorax or hyperinflation.
Relate findings to physiology: a hyperexpanded chest with prolonged expiration fits air trapping.
Follow your own medical school's mark scheme where its order differs.

interpret.title: Rate and rhythm on a lead II strip
interpret.q: Recorded at 25 mm/s: a regular rhythm with a P wave before every QRS. The R–R interval is 20 small squares, the PR interval 4 small squares and the QRS 2 small squares. What is the best description?
options: Sinus tachycardia at 150 beats/min
First-degree heart block at 75 beats/min
Sinus rhythm at 75 beats/min with normal intervals
Sinus bradycardia at 15 beats/min
interpret.why: Each small square is 0.04 s, so R–R = 0.8 s and rate = 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min (1,500 ÷ 20). PR = 0.16 s (normal 0.12–0.20 s) and QRS = 0.08 s (normal, under 0.12 s), with a P before every QRS: sinus rhythm. The QT of 0.38 s corrects (Bazett, QT ÷ √RR) to about 0.42 s, within the usual range (approximate).
optWhy: 150/min would need an R–R of 0.4 s (10 small squares); this treats each small square as 0.02 s, as at 50 mm/s.
First-degree block needs a PR over 0.20 s; 4 small squares is 0.16 s, which is normal.
Correct: R–R 0.8 s gives 75/min, with normal PR and QRS and a P before every QRS.
15/min comes from dividing 300 (the large-square rule) by the number of small squares.

interpret.title: Irregular palpitations
interpret.q: A 74-year-old has palpitations. The rhythm strip shows no distinct P waves and irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes, 18 of them in 10 seconds. Which interpretation fits?
options: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block at 150/min
Sinus arrhythmia at about 108/min
Atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 180/min
Atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 108/min
interpret.why: Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm is atrial fibrillation. For an irregular rhythm, count the complexes in 10 seconds and multiply by 6: 18 × 6 = 108/min. AF matters because stagnant blood in the atria can clot and embolise, causing stroke.
optWhy: Flutter shows regular sawtooth flutter waves and, with 2:1 block, a regular ventricular rate around 150/min.
Sinus arrhythmia has a P wave before every QRS and varies regularly with breathing.
180/min multiplies the 10-second count by 10 instead of 6.
Correct: no P waves, irregularly irregular, 18 × 6 = 108/min.

interpret.title: A long PR interval
interpret.q: A regular rhythm at 60/min with a P wave before every QRS. The PR interval is 7 small squares and constant; the QRS is 2 small squares. Where is conduction abnormal?
options: Failure of the SA node to fire
Slowed conduction through the AV node
Block in one bundle branch
Complete failure of conduction from atria to ventricles
interpret.why: PR = 7 × 0.04 = 0.28 s, longer than 0.20 s, but every P wave is conducted with the same interval: first-degree heart block, a delay in the AV node. The QRS (0.08 s) is narrow, so ventricular conduction is normal.
optWhy: SA node failure would cause missing P waves or pauses, not a long PR.
Correct: a constant PR over 0.20 s with every P conducted reflects AV nodal delay.
Bundle branch block widens the QRS to 0.12 s or more; here it is 0.08 s.
Complete block would leave P waves and QRS complexes unrelated, with no constant PR.

interpret.title: Dizzy spells and a slow pulse
interpret.q: An 82-year-old has dizzy spells. The strip shows regular P waves at 75/min and regular broad QRS complexes (0.14 s) at 35/min. The PR interval varies from beat to beat with no pattern. Which interpretation fits?
options: First-degree heart block
Sinus bradycardia
Complete heart block with a ventricular escape rhythm
Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response
interpret.why: P waves and QRS complexes are independent, so no atrial impulses reach the ventricles: complete (third-degree) heart block. A slow, broad-complex escape rhythm from below the block drives the ventricles. Because cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, the slow rate can lower blood pressure and cause dizziness.
optWhy: First-degree block has a constant (long) PR with every P conducted.
In sinus bradycardia each P wave is followed by a QRS at a fixed PR.
Correct: regular P waves and regular broad QRS complexes at different rates, with no fixed PR.
AF has no organised P waves and an irregular ventricular rhythm; here both are regular.

interpret.title: Pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 34-year-old has pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness; the sample was taken on air. Taking PIO₂ as 20 kPa and R as 0.8, which interpretation fits best? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Type 1 respiratory failure with an acute respiratory alkalosis and a raised A–a gradient (about 7.4 kPa)
Type 2 respiratory failure caused by hypoventilation
Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Respiratory alkalosis with a normal A–a gradient, so gas exchange is normal
interpret.why: PaO₂ is below 8 kPa with a low PaCO₂: type 1 respiratory failure. pH is high with low PaCO₂ and normal bicarbonate, an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. PAO₂ = 20 − 4.0/0.8 = 15.0 kPa, so the A–a gradient is 15.0 − 7.6 = 7.4 kPa, clearly raised: a gas-exchange problem such as V/Q mismatch (pulmonary embolism is one possibility with pleuritic pain).
optWhy: Correct: low PaO₂, low PaCO₂, high pH, normal bicarbonate and a raised A–a gradient.
Type 2 failure needs a raised PaCO₂; here it is low.
In a metabolic alkalosis bicarbonate would be raised and PaCO₂ would rise to compensate; here bicarbonate is normal and PaCO₂ low.
The A–a gradient is about 7.4 kPa, far above normal, so gas exchange is impaired.

interpret.title: Acutely breathless with long-standing COPD
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 70-year-old with long-standing COPD is more breathless than usual; the sample was taken on air. Which interpretation fits best? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Type 1 respiratory failure
Type 2 respiratory failure: respiratory acidosis with raised bicarbonate, suggesting acute-on-chronic CO₂ retention
Acute respiratory acidosis with no metabolic compensation
interpret.why: PaO₂ is below 8 kPa with a raised PaCO₂ (8.2 kPa ≈ 61.5 mmHg): type 2 respiratory failure. The low pH shows acidaemia of respiratory origin. Bicarbonate (30 mmol/L) is higher than an acute rise in CO₂ alone would give (roughly 26 mmol/L) and a little below what full chronic renal compensation would give (roughly 31–33 mmol/L). Chronic compensation is never complete, so even fully compensated chronic retention at this PaCO₂ would leave the pH only slightly low (about 7.32); a low pH alone cannot separate chronic from acute-on-chronic. The history of being more breathless than usual, with bicarbonate a little short of the chronic value, fits an acute worsening on top of chronic CO₂ retention (approximate rules of thumb). People at risk like this are the group for whom BTS sets a target saturation of 88–92%.
optWhy: A metabolic alkalosis would give a high pH; here pH is low.
Type 1 failure has a normal or low PaCO₂; here it is raised.
Correct: low pH, high PaCO₂, low PaO₂ and a raised bicarbonate.
Bicarbonate of 30 mmol/L is above what an acute rise alone would produce, so there is metabolic compensation from a chronic component.

interpret.title: Two weeks after starting an ACE inhibitor
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 66-year-old man had an ACE inhibitor started for hypertension two weeks ago; these are his repeat kidney function tests. Which explanation best fits the changes? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: Less aldosterone reduces renal potassium excretion, and loss of angiotensin II's constriction of the efferent arteriole lowers GFR slightly
ACE inhibitors cause potassium loss in the urine, so the high potassium must be a laboratory error
Bradykinin accumulation directly damages the renal tubules
Raised angiotensin II constricts the afferent arteriole and reduces GFR
interpret.why: Blocking angiotensin II production reduces aldosterone, so less K⁺ is excreted and potassium rises (here from 4.6 to 5.8 mmol/L). Angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole to support glomerular filtration pressure; removing it lowers GFR, so creatinine rises (95 to 118 µmol/L, about 24%). This is why kidney function and potassium are checked after starting these drugs; decisions on what to do are clinical and follow current guidance.
optWhy: Correct: both changes follow from the drug's mechanism.
ACE inhibitors tend to raise potassium, not lower it, so the result is consistent with the drug.
Bradykinin explains the cough, not these blood changes.
Angiotensin II falls, not rises, with an ACE inhibitor, and its main glomerular effect is on the efferent arteriole.

interpret.title: Breathless on exertion with normal saturation
interpret.rangeNote: Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.
interpret.q: A 42-year-old woman is breathless on exertion. SpO₂ is 98% on air and arterial PO₂ is normal. Using 1.34 mL O₂ per gram of haemoglobin and adding about 3 mL/L dissolved, what is her approximate arterial oxygen content, and why is she breathless? (Reference ranges shown are typical adult UK ranges and vary by laboratory.)
options: About 200 mL/L: normal, because her saturation is normal
About 11 mL/L: severe hypoxaemia
About 85 mL/L: oxygen content equals the haemoglobin concentration
About 115 mL/L: low haemoglobin reduces oxygen content and delivery despite normal saturation
interpret.why: Content ≈ 1.34 × 85 × 0.98 + 3 ≈ 115 mL/L, compared with about 200 mL/L at a haemoglobin of 150 g/L. Saturation and PaO₂ are normal, but there is less haemoglobin to carry oxygen, so delivery (cardiac output × content) falls on exertion. A low MCV (microcytic anaemia) most often reflects iron deficiency.
optWhy: About 200 mL/L is normal content at a haemoglobin of about 150 g/L; normal saturation does not mean normal content when haemoglobin is low.
About 11 is the content in mL per decilitre (using 8.5 g/dL); mixing units makes it look like 11 mL/L. Her PaO₂ is normal, so she is not hypoxaemic.
Content is not numerically equal to haemoglobin; each gram carries about 1.34 mL when fully saturated.
